lessons.title: Definition and Scope of Government
lessons.objective: Define government, distinguish it from the state, and explain why its scope covers the functions only public authority can perform.

content.heading: Government in one sentence
paragraphs: Government is the set of institutions that make, enforce and interpret binding rules for a society. Its scope is the work that needs public authority: keeping order, providing public goods and acting for the state.

content.heading: A bridge no business will rebuild
paragraphs: A bridge on a rural road collapses after heavy rain. Drivers cannot cross, farmers cannot move produce, and no private firm will rebuild it because it cannot charge every user. The council, state or federal agency with the road must act.

Government is the institution that makes, enforces and interprets the rules of a society. Its characteristics include a defined jurisdiction, a hierarchy of offices, taxing power and a claim to a monopoly on legitimate force.

It acts through three arms: the legislature makes law, the executive carries it out, and the judiciary settles disputes and interprets the law. Government is not the state; the state is the permanent political community of territory, population, government and sovereignty, while government is the replaceable machinery that rules it.
bullets: Government makes, enforces and interprets binding rules.
It has a defined jurisdiction and a hierarchy of offices.
It claims a monopoly on the legitimate use of force.
Its three arms are the legislature, executive and judiciary.
content.takeaway: Government is the ruling machinery of a permanent state.

check.question: Which of these is a characteristic of government rather than a function?
options: It has a defined jurisdiction and a hierarchy of offices.
It defends the country against attack.
check.why: A defined jurisdiction and hierarchy describe what government is; the others are services it provides.

content.heading: Why the bridge is not a business
paragraphs: Markets supply most of what people want: traders sell food, builders put up houses and banks lend money. Some goods are different. A defence force, a street light or a drainage system cannot easily be sold to one buyer, and everyone benefits whether they pay or not.

Government keeps law and order and protects life and property. It defends the territory, conducts relations with other states and provides public goods such as roads, schools, health care, water and security.
It also protects rights, regulates the economy and settles disputes. Taxes pay for these functions, which is why government must raise revenue.
bullets: Public goods are shared and hard to charge for, so markets under-supply them.
Government also protects rights and limits harm that markets ignore.
Taxes turn private income into shared public functions.
content.takeaway: Government does what markets cannot do fairly or profitably.

check.question: A private firm will not build a rural bridge because it cannot charge every user. Which function does this illustrate?
check.why: The bridge is shared and hard to charge for, so government supplies it as a public good.

content.heading: The coup that changed the government
paragraphs: In January 1966, soldiers took over Nigeria's government. The flag, territory, population and international borders stayed; the rulers changed. A coup replaces a government, not the state.

The state is the permanent political community: territory, population, government and sovereignty. Government is the temporary set of institutions that exercises the state's authority, which is why one state can have many governments.

The distinction also fixes the scope. Government acts for the state but does not own it, and its powers are limited by the constitution. In Nigeria, that scope is divided among federal, state and local tiers.
bullets: The state is permanent; a government is replaceable.
Government exercises the state's authority within constitutional limits.
Its scope is divided among federal, state and local tiers.
Public office is not private ownership.
content.takeaway: The state outlives the government that acts for it.

check.question: A coup removes a president and his ministers. What has changed?
check.why: A coup replaces rulers; the state's territory, population and sovereignty remain.

visual.caption: The state is the permanent community; the government is the machinery that rules it.

rows.left: Does it survive a change of rulers?
rows.right: Does it make and enforce rules?

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When a question asks about government, reject options that describe the state: permanent, sovereign, or defined by territory and population. Government is the replaceable machinery that makes and enforces rules for a society.

content.problem: Which statement best distinguishes government from the state? A. Government is permanent while the state changes B. The state is the ruling machinery while government is the community C. Government is the machinery that rules the state, which is permanent D. Government and the state are the same thing

steps.reason: The state is the permanent political community; government is the machinery that rules it.
steps.result: Look for an option that keeps that direction.
steps.predictPrompt: Which term survives a change of rulers?

steps.reason: The state survives changes of rulers, so any option calling government permanent is wrong.
steps.predictPrompt: What would a weaker answer look like here?

steps.reason: Government acts for the state; the state is not the machinery of government.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.question: A newly elected government promises to build roads, fund schools and defend the border. Explain why these are government functions rather than ordinary business activities. Then state one function that a private firm could perform.
hints: Ask whether the service can be sold to one buyer and withheld from others.
Defence and roads benefit people who do not pay, so markets under-supply them.
A private firm can build houses, sell food or run a bus service, but it needs the legal order that government maintains.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the state outlives its government
paragraphs: Permanence is a legal idea, not a physical one. A state continues when its government falls because its territory, population, constitution and international obligations continue. Other states recognise the state, not the regime.

This continuity matters in practice. Treaties signed by one government bind its successors, public debt survives a change of government, and civil servants, courts and police remain when ministers leave. A new government inherits both assets and obligations.

Sovereignty belongs to the state, not to the officeholder. The government exercises it for the time being: it makes treaties, declares war and passes laws, but it does not own the state's territory or people. That is why a coup can be illegal and still leave the state intact.

Exam questions often test this by asking what changes after a coup. The rulers change; the state's territory, population and sovereignty do not. The same logic explains why a country can lose its government without losing its statehood.
bullets: Treaties, debts and borders survive a change of government.
Sovereignty belongs to the state; the government exercises it temporarily.
A coup changes rulers, not statehood.

content.heading: Go deeper: Public goods and the limits of markets
paragraphs: A public good has two features: one person's use does not reduce another's, and non-payers cannot easily be excluded. Defence, street lighting and flood control are close examples. Because a firm cannot charge every beneficiary, it cannot recover the cost, so the good is under-supplied without public funding.

Some goods are not pure public goods but create externalities. A factory that pollutes imposes a cost on neighbours who did not agree to it. Government can tax the pollution, regulate the factory or require compensation, so that the private decision faces its social cost.

Other functions rest on coordination and trust. Courts settle disputes because private enforcement invites revenge, and standards for weights, measures and money reduce the cost of every transaction. Regulation of banks protects depositors who cannot inspect a balance sheet.

The scope is not unlimited. Government may fail too: monopolies can be inefficient, officials can be corrupt, and subsidies can outlive their purpose. The exam point is not that government should do everything, but that some functions cannot be left to a market alone.
bullets: Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable, so markets under-supply them.
Externalities and information gaps justify regulation.
Government failure limits what the state should attempt.

content.heading: Go deeper: Who does what in a federation
paragraphs: Nigeria divides government functions between federal, state and local tiers. The constitution lists exclusive functions for the federal government, such as defence, currency and foreign affairs. It lists concurrent functions for federal and state governments, such as education and health.

Residual functions go to the states, and local governments handle local services such as markets and refuse. The division is a scope rule. When a road is federal, a state government that rebuilds it may be acting outside its lane; when a market is local, the federal government should not run it directly.

In practice the tiers share costs and responsibilities, which blurs the line. States with more people and land may need more roads, while states with more taxable activity can raise more revenue. Federal transfers try to close the gap, but they also create dependence.
For exams, separate the two questions. First ask what the function is; then ask which tier has the power to perform it. A question about local government is usually testing the second.
bullets: Exclusive, concurrent and residual functions divide the tiers' scope.
The tier with the power may still share the cost.
Ask what the function is before asking who performs it.

lessons.title: Basic Concepts of Government
lessons.objective: Distinguish power, authority, legitimacy and sovereignty, and tell a state from a nation.

content.heading: Power, authority and the state
paragraphs: Power is the ability to make others act; authority is power accepted as rightful; legitimacy is the belief that justifies it. Sovereignty is supreme power, and a state is the political organisation that holds it over a territory and people.

content.heading: Power, authority and legitimacy
paragraphs: A coup leader controls the army and the radio but still needs people to accept his orders. Power is the ability to affect behaviour, even against resistance; influence shapes what others think without commanding them.

Authority is power accepted as rightful, and legitimacy is the belief that makes it rightful. Authority may be traditional, charismatic or legal-rational; modern states rely on the last, so authority attaches to the office rather than the person.
Power need not be legitimate. A government can hold office and still lose legitimacy, which is why legitimate governments need less coercion to collect taxes or enforce court orders.
bullets: Power compels; influence shapes; authority is accepted power.
Legitimacy is the belief that the right to rule is real.
Traditional, charismatic, legal-rational: authority's three sources.
content.takeaway: Legitimacy turns obedience from fear into duty.

check.question: The belief that a government has the right to rule is called ______.
check.why: Legitimacy is the belief; authority is power accepted as rightful because of that belief. Sovereignty is supreme authority, not the belief itself.

visual.caption: Legitimacy is the belief that turns power into authority.

rows.left: The ability to make others act

rows.right: Belief that the right to command is real
Do people obey because they accept the right?

rows.left: A coup leader with the army
rows.right: A government whose orders are accepted

content.heading: Sovereignty and the state
paragraphs: A state signs a treaty, and another state cannot overrule its courts. That independence abroad and supremacy at home is sovereignty.

Sovereignty is supreme and final authority within a territory. Internal sovereignty means the state is the highest authority over its people; external sovereignty means independence from other states. Legal sovereignty sits with the constitution or parliament, popular sovereignty with the people.

A state has territory, population, government and sovereignty. A nation is a people sharing an identity, and a nation-state exists when borders roughly match that identity. Nigeria is a state containing many nations; the Kurds are a nation without a state.
bullets: Internal: supremacy at home. External: independence abroad.
Legal sovereignty: constitution or parliament. Popular: the people.
State = territory + population + government + sovereignty.
content.takeaway: A state is a legal container; a nation is a community of belonging.

check.question: A state is distinguished from a nation by ______.
check.why: A state is defined by territory, population, government and sovereignty; a nation is defined by shared identity, which a state may contain several of.

content.heading: Political processes
paragraphs: A child learns to trust or suspect government at home, at school and through the media long before voting. That is political socialisation.

Political participation is activity through which people take part: voting, campaigning, protesting, contacting officials and standing for office. Political culture is the pattern of beliefs and values a society holds about politics, such as whether authority is trusted or suspected.
Socialisation forms attitudes, culture is the shared pattern they form, and participation expresses them. Low turnout can reflect apathy, but it can also reflect institutions that do not respond.
bullets: Socialisation forms attitudes; culture is the pattern; participation is the action.
Agents: family, school, media, religion, peers and parties.
content.takeaway: Socialisation explains how attitudes form; participation shows whether they are acted on.

check.question: The process by which people learn political attitudes and behaviour is ______.
check.why: Socialisation is the learning process; culture is the resulting pattern of beliefs, and participation is the activity itself.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When a question asks where authority is vested, name the source of legitimacy — the state or the people — not an agent such as the judiciary or the police.

content.problem: Political authority is vested in the ______.

steps.reason: Authority is legitimate power — the right to command.
steps.result: Find the body that owns political power, not one of its agents.
steps.predictPrompt: Is the judiciary the source of authority or an arm that exercises it?

steps.reason: The state holds sovereign authority over the political community.
steps.result: Authority is vested in the state.
steps.predictPrompt: What would a weaker answer look like here?

steps.reason: The judiciary, executive and armed forces exercise authority but do not own it.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test this answer before writing it down?

content.heading: Go deeper: Why legitimacy is harder to keep than to win
paragraphs: Legality and legitimacy are not the same. A law can be passed correctly and still be rejected as illegitimate if the process or the rulers are seen as unfair. Courts decide legality; people decide legitimacy. A government that confuses the two keeps winning cases while losing obedience.

Legitimacy has several sources. Input legitimacy comes from how power is won and exercised: free elections, the rule of law, consent. Output legitimacy comes from what government delivers: security, schools, roads, economic stability. A government can survive a deficit in one if the other is strong, but rarely both.

Coups expose the difference. A coup leader may control the army, the radio and the treasury — full power — yet lack authority, because no accepted rule makes his command rightful. To convert power into authority he must win recognition: from citizens, from other states, and often from an election.

Legitimacy is also cheaper than coercion. A legitimate government collects taxes, enforces court orders and recruits soldiers with less force, because people comply voluntarily. Once legitimacy erodes, every policy costs more to enforce.
bullets: Legality is decided by courts; legitimacy is decided by belief and consent.
Input legitimacy comes from how power is won; output legitimacy from what it delivers.
A coup can seize power without acquiring authority.
Legitimacy lowers the cost of governing because compliance becomes voluntary.

content.heading: Go deeper: Sovereignty in a world of interdependence
paragraphs: Sovereignty sounds absolute, but no modern state exercises it without limits. A state joins the United Nations and accepts its charter; it signs treaties that bind future governments; it borrows money on conditions set by lenders. Each commitment is a voluntary limit on external sovereignty.

Pooled sovereignty is the formal name for this. Members of ECOWAS, the African Union and the United Nations delegate some decisions to collective bodies in exchange for influence and protection. Nigeria can shape ECOWAS decisions, but it must also accept decisions it dislikes.

Internal sovereignty is constrained too. Federalism divides authority between national and state governments; constitutions entrench rights that no majority may remove; independent courts can strike down laws. These are not failures of sovereignty but its organisation.

Economic dependence adds a harder limit. Debt service, import dependence and foreign investment give outsiders leverage over budgets and policy. A state may be legally sovereign and still have little room to choose.
bullets: Treaties and international organisations voluntarily limit external sovereignty.
Federalism, entrenched rights and judicial review divide internal sovereignty by design.
Legal sovereignty does not guarantee policy freedom when the economy is dependent.

content.heading: Go deeper: Reading political culture and participation
paragraphs: Political culture is not opinion polling. It is the durable pattern of beliefs about authority, participation and the state. Almond and Verba distinguished parochial culture, where people barely identify with the state; subject culture, where they obey but do not participate; and participant culture, where they expect to influence decisions.

Most states mix the three. A village may be parochial about national politics while a capital city is participant. The mix explains why the same constitution produces different behaviour in different places.

Participation is shaped by resources and institutions. Educated, urban and organised citizens vote, lobby and protest more; proportional systems and strong parties raise turnout; repression lowers it. Low turnout is therefore not always apathy — it can be a rational response to institutions that do not respond.
For exams, keep the map clean: socialisation explains how attitudes form, culture describes the pattern, participation describes the action.
bullets: Parochial, subject and participant cultures differ in whether people identify, obey or engage.
Most states contain a mixture of cultures rather than one pure type.
Participation tracks resources and institutions, not just individual interest.
Socialisation → culture → participation is the causal chain to remember.

content.question: A traditional ruler is obeyed because people believe his office is rightful. Is that power, authority or legitimacy? Explain in one sentence.
hints: Power is the ability to influence; authority is accepted power.
The people accept the office as rightful — that belief is legitimacy.
The best answer names authority and explains that legitimacy is the belief supporting it.

lessons.title: Forms of Government: Who Rules?
lessons.objective: Distinguish democracy, monarchy, aristocracy, oligarchy, autocracy and the republic, and give the features, merits and demerits of each.

content.heading: Form in one sentence
paragraphs: A form of government answers one question: who holds ruling power, and on what claim?

content.heading: A ballot box and an elected president
paragraphs: One country elects a president every four years; another keeps a king who reigns but does not rule. Both can be democratic, because the test is whether the people choose and can remove their rulers, not the title at the top.

Democracy is rule by the people, exercised directly in a town meeting or, more commonly, through elected representatives. Its features are free and fair elections, majority rule with minority rights, the rule of law, accountability and a free press.

Its merits are participation, legitimacy and peaceful change; its demerits are slow decisions, the risk of majority tyranny and the cost of elections. Republicanism is narrower: an elected head of state instead of a hereditary monarch, and a republic may still be undemocratic.
bullets: Democracy: the people choose and can remove their rulers.
Features: free elections, rule of law, accountability, minority rights.
Republic: an elected head of state, not a hereditary monarch.
content.takeaway: Democracy is measured by choice and removal, not by the ruler's title.

check.question: A state has an elected president and no hereditary monarch. Its form is a ______.
check.why: An elected head of state without a hereditary monarch is a republic; whether it is democratic depends on elections and rights.

content.heading: A crown, a council of nobles, a wealthy few
paragraphs: A king inherits the throne, a council of nobles claims to rule because of birth and virtue, and a handful of wealthy families controls the state. The first is monarchy, the second aristocracy, the third oligarchy.

Monarchy is rule by one person, usually hereditary; it is absolute when the monarch rules and constitutional when the monarch reigns but a parliament governs. Aristocracy is rule by a small group claiming superior birth or education. Oligarchy is rule by a few, often through wealth, family or force; plutocracy is rule by the rich.

Monarchy offers continuity and clear succession, but suffers disputed successions and weak accountability. Aristocracy can draw on experience, yet excludes outsiders; oligarchy can decide quickly, but serves a narrow interest.
bullets: Monarchy: one hereditary ruler; absolute or constitutional.
Aristocracy: the few who claim to be best.
Oligarchy: the few who hold wealth or force.
content.takeaway: The three differ in who rules and on what claim.

check.question: Rule by a small group considered the best is called ______.
check.why: Aristocracy claims rule by the best; oligarchy is rule by a few without that claim, and gerontocracy is rule by the old.

content.heading: One man, the elders, the priests
paragraphs: One man rules by decree; elsewhere only elders may hold office; in another state, priests interpret the law. Autocracy, gerontocracy and theocracy each concentrate power, but they justify it differently.

Autocracy is one person with unlimited power, checked by no institution; dictatorship is its modern form. Gerontocracy gives power to the oldest, theocracy to religious authority, and a military junta to a council of officers. Mobocracy is rule by an unruly crowd, which is disorder rather than a constitution.

Autocracy can act quickly in a crisis, but it lacks accountability and peaceful succession. Gerontocracy respects age and memory, but excludes the young; theocracy offers divine legitimacy, but narrows dissent; a junta can restore order, but rarely wins legitimacy.
bullets: Autocracy: one ruler with unlimited power.
Gerontocracy: rule by the old; theocracy: rule by religious authority.
Military junta: a council of officers; mobocracy: rule by the crowd.
content.takeaway: Concentrated power differs in who holds it and how it is justified.

check.question: A form of government organised by a council of military officers is called a ______.
check.why: The officers' council in power is a junta; stratocracy is the wider term for military rule.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Form = who rules. System = how the executive and legislature relate. A republic is not automatically a democracy, and a constitutional monarch reigns but does not rule.

content.problem: Classify each case: (a) a queen whose parliament makes the laws; (b) a council of elders who hold office because of their age; (c) a general who suspends the constitution and rules by decree.

steps.reason: A hereditary head of state who reigns while parliament governs is a constitutional monarch.
steps.predictPrompt: Who holds office because of age?

steps.reason: Power reserved for the oldest is gerontocracy.
steps.predictPrompt: What could go wrong at this step, and how do you prevent it?

steps.reason: A council of officers ruling without the constitution is a military junta.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.question: Nigeria is a republic with an elected president. Explain why it is also a democracy, and name one feature that would be missing under a military junta.
hints: A republic names the head of state; democracy describes how rulers are chosen and removed.
Elections, accountability and minority rights are the democratic tests.
A junta would remove free elections and accountability to the legislature.

content.heading: Go deeper: Aristocracy, oligarchy and the claim of the few
paragraphs: Both terms describe rule by a small group, so questions test the claim each makes. Aristocracy means rule by those regarded as the best, through birth, education or virtue. Oligarchy means rule by a few through wealth, family or force, without claiming special merit.

Plutocracy narrows oligarchy to the rich, as when only people above a property threshold may stand for office. An aristocratic council may instead draw on experts, chiefs or senior officials whose claim is competence. Examiners separate the source of the claim from the number of rulers.

Gerontocracy, theocracy, stratocracy and junta name other small-group claims. Gerontocracy reserves office for the old, theocracy for religious authority and stratocracy for military command. A junta is officers governing as a council. Mobocracy is an unruly crowd; it is disorder, not a constitution.

Nigeria shows why the distinction survives criticism of a narrow circle. A republic with an elected president keeps that form even when a strong executive or dominant party is called oligarchic in everyday speech. The test remains who holds power and on what claim.
bullets: Aristocracy claims rule by the best.
Oligarchy is rule by a few through wealth or force.
Plutocracy, gerontocracy, theocracy and stratocracy name different claims.
A junta is officers governing; mob rule is disorder.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why a democracy can look democratic and act otherwise
paragraphs: Democracy depends on more than counting votes. Free and fair elections choose rulers, but the rule of law, freedom of expression, a free press and accountable institutions decide whether those rulers remain removable. When courts are ignored, journalists are harassed or election bodies are captured, the ballot may still take place while the possibility of genuine change shrinks.

Majority rule creates a special danger. A majority that can pass any law and punish any minority turns popular consent into a weapon. That is why democratic constitutions protect rights that a simple majority cannot remove, such as freedom of expression and association. Minority rights are not a decoration on democracy; they are the reason a majority must govern within limits.

Accountability is the day-to-day mechanism. Ministers answer to the legislature, officials justify spending, courts strike down unlawful acts and the press exposes failure. Each channel is separate, so a defect in one does not automatically destroy the others. A state can hold regular elections and still lose accountability when every channel points to the same office.

Nigeria illustrates the distinction between republic and democracy. The republic describes an elected president instead of a hereditary ruler, while the democratic test asks whether elections are free, rights are protected and rulers can be removed in practice. A republic without those features is a republic but not yet a democratic one, which is exactly the confusion many questions try to create.
bullets: Elections without courts, a free press and protected rights are a thin democracy.
Minority rights stop a majority from ruling without limits.
Accountability runs through the legislature, courts, auditors and the press.
Republic names the head of state; democracy names how rulers are chosen, limited and removed.

content.heading: Go deeper: Constitutional monarchy, absolute rule and the cost of succession
paragraphs: Monarchy divides into constitutional and absolute forms because the title matters less than the power. A constitutional monarch reigns but does not govern: ministers rule, parliament makes law and the monarch performs ceremonial duties under the constitution. An absolute monarch rules directly, makes law and controls the executive, so no institution can overrule the throne.

Hereditary succession explains both the attraction and the weakness. It promises continuity because the next ruler is known at birth, yet it offers no test of fitness. A child, an incapable adult or a disputed succession can therefore create a crisis that an elected office avoids by separating succession from family. That is why some monarchies appoint a regent or a council to act while the heir is young or disputed.

Autocracy concentrates the same problem in one person without the hereditary claim. Power is unlimited, institutions are checked by the ruler rather than the reverse, and succession depends on force or favour. A coup leader who suspends the constitution and governs by decree is not a monarch by birth, but the absence of accountability places that government close to autocracy. A junta spreads that power among officers without making it accountable.

The exam rule is to ask about power before title. If parliament governs, call the arrangement constitutional monarchy even when a queen or king is present. If one person or a council rules without the constitution, focus on the absence of choice and check rather than the uniform, the palace or the family name.
bullets: Constitutional monarch reigns while ministers and parliament govern.
Hereditary succession gives continuity but no guarantee of fitness.
Autocracy and junta rule differ in personnel, not in accountability.
Ask who can overrule the ruler before naming the form.

lessons.title: Arms of Government
lessons.objective: Match each arm to its types, functions and powers, and explain how the three arms check one another.

content.heading: Three arms, one government
paragraphs: The legislature makes law, the executive implements it, and the judiciary interprets it. Separation of powers also lets each arm check the others, so no arm governs alone.

content.heading: A bill on rural roads
paragraphs: A senator proposes a bill to fund rural roads. It is introduced, debated, examined in committee and passed by both chambers. Assent turns it into an Act; a veto can be overridden.

The legislature is the law-making arm. It may be unicameral, with one chamber, or bicameral, with two. Nigeria's National Assembly has a Senate and a House of Representatives, and each state has a House of Assembly.

It makes, amends and repeals laws, approves the budget, oversees public spending and represents constituencies; the Senate confirms appointments. A bill passes first reading, second reading, committee stage and third reading before assent.
In Britain Parliament is supreme; in Nigeria the Constitution is supreme, so the National Assembly cannot make any law it likes.
bullets: The legislature makes, amends and repeals laws.
Nigeria has a bicameral National Assembly: Senate and House of Representatives.
Debate begins at second reading; assent makes a bill an Act.
content.takeaway: The legislature makes law, but assent and the Constitution limit it.

check.question: At which stage does debate on a bill begin?
check.why: First reading is a formal introduction; debate begins at second reading.

content.heading: The ministry must build the road
paragraphs: The Act is law, but the road is still unbuilt. A ministry plans it, the civil service drafts the contract, and the police keep order. The executive turns law into action.

The executive implements laws and runs the country day to day. It may be presidential, with a president who is both head of state and government, or parliamentary, with a prime minister leading a cabinet from the legislature.
It conducts foreign relations, defends the territory, prepares the budget and appoints officials. It checks the legislature through assent and veto, and it makes delegated legislation under statute.

The civil service is the permanent body of officials in ministries; it is part of the wider public service, which also includes the police, armed forces and parastatals. Implementing government programmes is its primary duty.
bullets: The executive implements laws and runs government day to day.
Political executive = elected ministers; administrative executive = civil service.
Civil service = permanent ministry officials; public service = the wider body.
content.takeaway: The executive turns law into administration.

check.question: The executive checks the legislature mainly through ______.
check.why: The president can sign or withhold assent; treaties and orders are other executive powers.

content.heading: The court reads the Act
paragraphs: A contractor is denied payment and sues the ministry. The court reads the Act, examines the minister's decision and orders payment. It interpreted the law and checked the executive.

The judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes. Its components are the courts: the Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, Federal High Court, State High Courts, Sharia and Customary Courts of Appeal, and tribunals.

It interprets the Constitution, protects rights, punishes offenders and reviews government action. Judicial review lets it declare a law or executive act unconstitutional, which checks both other arms.

Judicial independence means judges decide without legislative or executive pressure. Security of tenure, salaries charged to the Consolidated Revenue Fund and appointment through the Federal Judicial Service Commission and National Judicial Council protect it.
bullets: The judiciary interprets laws, protects rights and reviews government action.
Judicial review can void an unconstitutional law or executive act.
Independence means no legislative or executive pressure on decisions.
FJSC nominates federal judges; NJC recommends them to the President.
content.takeaway: The judiciary interprets the law and checks both other arms.

check.question: The independence of the judiciary means that ______.
options: judges must ignore legislative and executive affairs
court decisions cannot be reviewed by any higher court
legislative and executive influence on judicial decisions must be prevented
judges must be protected from public criticism
check.why: Independence protects the decision, not the judge from criticism or appeal.

visual.caption: A bill crosses all three arms: the legislature passes it, the executive assents and implements, the courts interpret.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In Nigeria the Constitution is supreme, not the legislature. A bill needs both chambers and presidential assent, or an override of a veto; a court can later strike down the Act if it conflicts with the Constitution.

content.problem: A bill passes both chambers but the president refuses assent. What happens next? A. It becomes law after thirty days B. It fails unless the National Assembly overrides the veto C. The Supreme Court signs it D. State governors assent

steps.reason: The bill has passed both chambers but lacks assent.
steps.result: It is not yet an Act.
steps.predictPrompt: Who signs a federal bill into law?

steps.reason: A two-thirds majority of each chamber can override a presidential veto.
steps.result: The bill can still become law.
steps.predictPrompt: What would a weaker answer look like here?

steps.reason: Courts do not sign bills and governors do not assent to federal bills.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you prove this claim to a sceptic?

content.question: Name the arm that makes laws and the arm that implements them. Then explain one check each arm has on the other.
hints: The legislature makes law; the executive implements it.
The executive can assent to or veto a bill; the legislature can override a veto or refuse to confirm appointments.
The judiciary can review both laws and executive action.

content.heading: Go deeper: How a bill becomes law in Nigeria
paragraphs: A bill is a proposed law. In Nigeria, it may be introduced in either chamber of the National Assembly, except a money bill, which starts in the House of Representatives.

The first reading is a formal introduction; no debate takes place. Debate begins at the second reading, where members discuss the general principles. The committee stage then examines the clauses in detail, and the report stage brings the amended bill back to the chamber.
The third reading is the final passage vote. The other chamber must concur, and any disagreement is resolved by a conference committee. The bill then goes to the president for assent.

If the president withholds assent, he returns it with reasons. The National Assembly can override the veto by a two-thirds majority of each chamber, and the bill becomes law. A state bill follows the same path through the State House of Assembly and the governor.
Courts do not make the bill law, but they may later interpret it or declare it unconstitutional. That is why the process is a chain across the three arms, not a single legislative act.
bullets: First reading introduces; second reading debates; committee stage examines clauses.
Both chambers must agree before assent.
A two-thirds majority in each chamber can override a presidential veto.

content.heading: Go deeper: Presidential and parliamentary executives
paragraphs: In a presidential system, the president is both head of state and head of government, and the executive is separately elected from the legislature. In a parliamentary system, the prime minister is head of government while a monarch or ceremonial president is head of state.

The parliamentary executive is drawn from the legislature and survives only while it holds the confidence of the majority. A vote of no confidence can bring it down, and the prime minister may dissolve parliament and call an election. The presidential executive has a fixed term and cannot be removed by a simple vote of no confidence.

Nigeria operates a presidential system: the president is elected separately, appoints ministers with Senate confirmation, and serves a fixed four-year term. Britain operates a parliamentary system: the prime minister normally leads the party with a majority in the House of Commons.

The difference shapes the checks. A presidential president can veto legislation but may face an override; a prime minister usually controls the legislative programme because the executive sits in the legislature. Neither system removes the need for judicial review.
bullets: Presidential: separate election, fixed term, president is head of state and government.
Parliamentary: executive from the legislature; a confidence vote can remove it.
Nigeria is presidential; Britain is parliamentary.

content.heading: Go deeper: Judicial independence and the appointment of judges
paragraphs: Judicial independence has two sides: the courts must be free from interference, and judges must be accountable to the law. Nigeria protects the first through security of tenure, salaries charged to the Consolidated Revenue Fund, and a disciplined removal process.

Federal judicial appointments begin with the Federal Judicial Service Commission, which advises the National Judicial Council on nominees. The NJC recommends candidates to the President, and the Senate confirms the senior federal appointments, including the Chief Justice of Nigeria and the justices of the Supreme Court.

State appointments follow a similar path through the State Judicial Service Commission and the governor, with the NJC involved and the State House of Assembly confirming the Chief Judge. The process is designed to keep patronage out of the bench, though critics say it remains political.

Independence does not mean judges ignore the law or answer to no one. They can be removed for misconduct, and their decisions can be appealed. What it forbids is a president or legislature punishing a judge for an unpopular ruling.

The judiciary also checks the other arms through judicial review. It can declare a statute unconstitutional, quash an executive action, or order a public body to act lawfully. That power is strongest when judges are seen to be independent, because a ruling that looks politically dictated loses authority.
bullets: Tenure, protected salaries and a removal process shield judges from pressure.
The FJSC advises; the NJC recommends; the Senate confirms senior appointments.
Independence means freedom from interference, not freedom from the law.

lessons.title: Constitution: Sources, Types and Supremacy
lessons.objective: Explain what a constitution is, identify its sources and types, and show why it is supreme over ordinary law.

content.heading: Constitution in one sentence
paragraphs: A constitution is the fundamental law that creates public offices and limits them; everything else must comply with it.

content.heading: The rulebook a government cannot ignore
paragraphs: A new government wants to detain a critic without trial. It cannot simply order the police to act, because the constitution sets the procedure and the courts can strike the order down. That is what makes it fundamental law.

A constitution creates the main institutions, distributes their powers, limits what they may do, protects rights and gives the regime legitimacy. Its sources include the constitutional text itself, statutes, judicial precedents, conventions, customary law and international treaties.

It also fixes offices and qualifications. The 1979 Constitution required a presidential candidate to be at least 35, a rule the 1999 Constitution keeps. Under the 1999 Constitution the Attorney-General is the Chief Law Officer, while the Chief Justice heads the Supreme Court.
bullets: Creates institutions, distributes power, limits government.
Sources: text, statutes, case law, conventions, custom, treaties.
Fixes qualifications and offices.
content.takeaway: A constitution is law about government, not a policy manifesto.

check.question: The fundamental laws of a country are contained in its ______.
check.why: The constitution is the fundamental law; manifestoes and edicts are party or military instruments, not the fundamental law.

content.heading: Written or unwritten, rigid or flexible
paragraphs: Britain has no single document called a constitution; its rules sit in statutes, court decisions and conventions. The United States has one written document that is hard to amend. Both are constitutional, but they are different types.

A written constitution is codified in one document; an unwritten one is scattered across statutes, precedents and conventions. A rigid constitution needs a special procedure to amend; a flexible one can be changed by ordinary law. Nigeria's is written and rigid; Britain's is unwritten and flexible.

Written constitutions give certainty and protect rights, but they can be rigid and litigation-heavy. Unwritten ones adapt easily, but they are uncertain and depend on convention. Federal states usually need a written constitution to protect the units.
bullets: Written: one document. Unwritten: statutes, cases and conventions.
Rigid: special amendment. Flexible: ordinary law.
Nigeria written and rigid; Britain unwritten and flexible.
content.takeaway: The written/unwritten line is about form; rigid/flexible is about amendment.

check.question: An example of a country with an unwritten constitution is ______.
check.why: The United Kingdom has no single codified constitution; Nigeria, the United States and Sierra Leone have written constitutions.

content.heading: The constitution is supreme
paragraphs: A state assembly passes a law allowing detention without trial. A court voids it, because the constitution says any law inconsistent with it is void to the extent of the inconsistency. That is supremacy.

Supremacy means the constitution ranks above ordinary legislation, and courts can review both laws and executive acts for consistency. It limits power, protects rights and gives citizens a fixed standard, but it also makes change slow and can hand large decisions to judges.
The alternative is legislative supremacy, where parliament is the highest law-maker and courts cannot void its statutes. Britain works this way; Nigeria does not.
bullets: Inconsistent law is void to that extent.
Courts review laws and executive acts.
Nigeria: constitutional supremacy; Britain: legislative supremacy.
content.takeaway: Supremacy decides who has the last word: the constitution or the legislature.

check.question: A state law conflicts with the constitution. What happens?
options: It stands because the assembly passed it
It is void to the extent of the inconsistency
The president decides whether it stands
It stands until the assembly amends it
check.why: Constitutional supremacy voids an inconsistent law to that extent; the assembly cannot override the constitution by ordinary legislation.

visual.caption: Supremacy is a test, not a slogan: the court measures each law against the constitution.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Written is not the same as rigid, and unwritten is not the same as flexible. Britain is unwritten but flexible; Nigeria is written and rigid.

content.problem: Classify each constitution: (a) one codified document amended only by a special majority; (b) rules spread across statutes, cases and conventions; (c) a codified document that an ordinary Act of Parliament can amend.

steps.reason: One codified document with a special amendment procedure is written and rigid.
steps.predictPrompt: What type has no single document?

steps.reason: Rules spread across sources, with no single codified text, make an unwritten constitution.
steps.predictPrompt: What would a weaker answer look like here?

steps.reason: A codified text amendable by ordinary law is written but flexible.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.question: Why does a federal state usually need a written and rigid constitution, and what does that rigidity cost?
hints: A written text protects the units' powers from the centre.
Rigidity stops a simple majority from rewriting the bargain.
The cost is slow amendment and heavy reliance on courts.

content.heading: Go deeper: How supremacy is tested in a Nigerian court
paragraphs: Supremacy becomes real when someone argues that a law does not fit the constitution. A detained critic, a state claiming a federal power or a trader taxed contrary to free movement can ask a court to measure the act against the text. The court asks about consistency, not policy preference.

The remedy is precise rather than destructive. The court declares the inconsistent part void to the extent of the inconsistency, so the remainder of the statute may stand. An executive order without constitutional backing may fall entirely. Only the offending rule is removed.

Nigeria provides several forums. The Federal High Court and State High Courts hear many rights cases, the Court of Appeal corrects errors of law and the Supreme Court gives final authority. The Attorney-General of the Federation is the Chief Law Officer, while the Chief Justice heads the Supreme Court.

The National Assembly is bound as well. It cannot use ordinary legislation to abolish a protected right or transfer a residual power to the centre. A law passed by both chambers and assented to by the President can still be void if it conflicts with the constitution.
bullets: A court measures a law against the constitution, not against preference.
An inconsistent law is void to the extent of the inconsistency.
Federal High Court, State High Courts, Court of Appeal and Supreme Court form the path.
Even an assented federal law can fall if it conflicts with the constitution.

content.heading: Go deeper: Codification, convention and the price of rigidity
paragraphs: Written and unwritten describe where rules sit, while rigid and flexible describe how they change. Nigeria places its main rules in one codified document that can only be amended by a special procedure, so it is written and rigid. Britain keeps much of its constitution across statutes, court decisions and conventions, and can change most of it by ordinary legislation, so it is unwritten and flexible.

Conventions show why an unwritten system can still be stable. A convention may not be enforceable in court, yet ministers, parliament and the courts treat it as binding because breaking it would damage trust in the whole arrangement. Codification trades that flexibility for certainty: everyone can read the allocation of powers, but reform must follow the stated procedure rather than ordinary majority voting.

Rigidity protects a bargain. In a diverse federation, the centre and the states can accept a division of powers only if a temporary majority cannot rewrite it at will. Exclusive, concurrent and residual functions are therefore likely to be entrenched, because each tier needs assurance that the other will not capture the bargain after an election or a census dispute.

The price is delay and litigation. A rigid text may keep an imperfect rule long after circumstances change, and disputes over its meaning move to court. Flexible constitutions amend quickly but risk instability when a majority rewrites the rules after every contest. Neither option is automatically democratic; each simply locates the difficulty in a different place.
bullets: Written is about one document; rigid is about a special amendment procedure.
Conventions bind through practice even when courts cannot enforce them.
Rigidity protects the federal bargain from a temporary majority.
The cost of rigidity is slow reform and heavier reliance on courts.

content.heading: Go deeper: Where a constitution draws its authority
paragraphs: A constitution claims authority from more than its own words. The text creates offices and distributes powers, while statutes add detail, court decisions give the text a working meaning and conventions grow around brief clauses. Customary practice also survives unless the constitution displaces it. Treaties add obligations the state has accepted.

Precedent is the engine of that development. When a higher court explains a clause, later courts normally follow the explanation, so one case can shape how detention, taxation or federal powers are understood for years. A constitution is therefore the document as interpreted, amended and practised over time.

Federal character shows how procedure creates legitimacy. In a country of many ethnic and regional groups, the 1999 Constitution as amended spreads federal offices and resources so no section owns the centre. Appointment and allocation must visibly recognise diversity, or the bargain loses the consent that sustains it.

Military rule reveals the opposite condition. A regime that suspends parts of the constitution and governs by decree may run the state, but it breaks the chain from text to consent. When civilian institutions return, courts must decide which acts followed the constitution and which did not.
bullets: Text, statutes, precedent, convention, custom and treaties feed meaning.
Precedent turns clauses into a working rule.
Federal character is a legitimacy device.
Suspension by decree breaks consent even when administration continues.

lessons.title: Pre-colonial Nigerian Polities
lessons.objective: Compare the Yoruba monarchy, the Igbo assembly system and the Hausa/Fulani emirate, and explain how each organised authority.

content.heading: Pre-colonial polities in one sentence
paragraphs: Before colonial rule, the Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa/Fulani organised government in three different ways.

content.heading: The Yoruba monarchy
paragraphs: An Alaafin of Oyo does not rule alone: he governs with a council of chiefs that can check him. That division is the mark of the Yoruba political system.

The Yoruba were monarchical. The Oba or Alaafin ruled with the Oyomesi, the council of senior chiefs, and the Ogboni cult, which handled religious and judicial matters and could restrain a tyrannical ruler.

The system combined a central palace with checks: the Oyomesi advised the Oba, and the Ogboni judged serious cases. Power was hierarchical but not absolute. A ruler who ignored both bodies risked deposition.
bullets: Head: Oba or Alaafin.
Council: Oyomesi.
Ogboni: religious and judicial check.
content.takeaway: The Yoruba system was monarchical, but the monarchy was checked by council and cult.

check.question: The traditional political system of the Yoruba kingdom was ______.
check.why: A central Oba or Alaafin ruled through the Oyomesi and Ogboni; the other labels describe systems without a hereditary throne.

content.heading: The Igbo assembly
paragraphs: An Igbo village settles a land dispute in an open assembly, and no single ruler pronounces the verdict. The community decides.

The Igbo were largely acephalous, meaning they had no single paramount ruler. The village assembly, Oha-na-eze, debated issues; the Okpara, the oldest man, presided; age grades enforced decisions and title societies conferred prestige.

Authority was diffused and decisions were reached by consensus. That made the system flexible and participatory, but it also meant colonial officers could find no single chief to sign a treaty with. They appointed warrant chiefs instead, and the innovation caused conflict.
bullets: Acephalous: no paramount ruler.
Oha-na-eze: village assembly.
Okpara: oldest man; age grades and title societies.
content.takeaway: The Igbo system governed through assembly and consensus rather than a throne.

check.question: The most senior member of the council of elders in the Igbo political system was the ______.
check.why: The Okpara was the oldest man who presided over the assembly; Obi and Eze are titles in other systems, and Ofo is a symbol of authority.

visual.caption: Both systems checked power, but one through a throne and the other through an assembly.

content.heading: The Hausa/Fulani emirate
paragraphs: An Emir sits in his palace, appoints district heads and judges cases under Islamic law. The emirate is both a government and a religious order.
The Hausa/Fulani system was theocratic and centralised. The Emir ruled by Islamic law, the Galadima administered the capital, the Madaki commanded the army and the Alkali judged cases.

Not every northern group was organised this way. The Tiv, for example, had a non-centralised system and were not influenced by Islamic political culture in the same way as the Kanuri, Fulani and Nupe. The emirates shared a single religious and legal framework, which is why the Tiv stand out.
bullets: Emir: ruler under Islamic law.
Galadima: capital. Madaki: army. Alkali: judge.
Tiv: the non-Islamic exception in the north.
content.takeaway: The emirate fused political and religious authority in one ruler.

check.question: The Galadima in the emirate system was ______.
options: officer in charge of the army
check.why: The Galadima administered the capital; the Alkali judged and the Madaki commanded the army.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: The three systems are not a ranking. Monarchy, acephalous consensus and theocratic centralisation are different answers to the same problem of order.

content.problem: Classify each scene: (a) an Alaafin meets the Oyomesi before a decision; (b) a village assembly debates a land case until agreement; (c) an Emir appoints a district head and an Alkali to hear a case.

steps.reason: A hereditary ruler advised by the Oyomesi is the Yoruba monarchy.
steps.predictPrompt: Which system decides by consensus?

steps.reason: An open assembly reaching agreement without a paramount ruler is the Igbo system.
steps.predictPrompt: Which part of the question does this step answer?

steps.reason: An Emir appointing officials and a judge under Islamic law is the Hausa/Fulani emirate.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.question: Why did indirect rule work more easily in the emirates than in Igboland?
hints: Indirect rule needed a single authority through whom the district officer could govern.
The emirate already had a hierarchy of district and village heads.
Igbo consensus government left no paramount chief, so the British created warrant chiefs.

content.heading: Go deeper: Three answers to the problem of a bad ruler
paragraphs: Every pre-colonial system had to solve the same practical problem: what happens when the person in charge becomes unjust? The Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa/Fulani solutions differed because each located authority in a different place. Their differences are clearer when each is read as a device for restraint rather than as a simple story about who was in charge.

In Yoruba kingdoms the Oba or Alaafin ruled from a palace but not alone. The Oyomesi acted as a senior council that advised and could resist, while the Ogboni combined religious standing with judicial functions and could restrain a ruler who ignored counsel. A ruler who treated both bodies as ornaments risked deposition, so hierarchy carried a built-in warning. Power moved through a centre that had to listen.

Igbo communities removed the centre itself. The village assembly, presided over by the Okpara as the oldest man, argued until consensus emerged, while age grades enforced the result and title societies gave prestige without creating a throne. That design prevented a single tyrant but slowed decisions and left no obvious signatory. The absence of a paramount ruler was itself the restraint.

The Hausa/Fulani emirates placed restraint inside a centralised order. The Emir ruled under Islamic law, the Galadima managed the capital, the Madaki handled military command and the Alkali judged cases. Authority looked absolute from a distance, yet it ran through named offices with distinct duties. A lower head could administer, command or judge without becoming the Emir, because the offices defined the limits.
bullets: Yoruba restraint ran through the Oyomesi and the Ogboni.
Igbo restraint removed a single centre and required consensus.
Emirate restraint ran through named offices under Islamic law.
Each system solved tyranny by placing authority in a different location.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why indirect rule fitted the emirates and strained Igboland
paragraphs: Indirect rule was, for colonial officers, an administrative shortcut. Instead of governing every village directly, a district officer ruled through an existing hierarchy that collected taxes, kept order and supplied information. Where that hierarchy already existed, the claims of chiefs and the needs of the colonial state could be made to point in the same direction.

The emirates supplied that hierarchy with unusual clarity. An Emir at the top, district heads below and alkali courts for judgement gave officers a chain they could recognise and use. The colonial state could therefore present itself as the protector of the emirate order while quietly taking control of its external relations. Centralisation made the bargain visible on both sides.

Igbo assembly government offered no equivalent chain. Decisions emerged from the Oha-na-eze after wide debate, enforcement ran through age grades and prestige through title societies, but no single chief could bind the whole area. Officers who needed one partner therefore created warrant chiefs through warrants issued by the colonial authority. Those appointments invented a form of paramountcy that the assembly system had deliberately avoided.

The result was not simply that Igboland was harder to govern. It was that indirect rule changed what it touched. In the emirates it worked through institutions that already commanded obedience; in Igboland it manufactured an authority that lacked the older consent. That contrast explains why the warrant system attracted resistance while the emirate hierarchy endured longer within the colonial structure.
bullets: Indirect rule needed an existing hierarchy it could rule through.
Emirate offices gave the colonial state a ready chain of command.
Warrant chiefs created paramountcy where consensus had avoided it.
The same policy strengthened one system and invented another.

content.heading: Go deeper: The Tiv and the danger of calling the North one thing
paragraphs: Nigeria is often described through three great systems, but the description can mislead if it treats every group in the north as an emirate. The Hausa/Fulani emirates shared Islamic law, a central throne and ranked offices, yet the Tiv organised authority without a comparable central ruler and without the same Islamic political culture. That single exception changes the map.

The Kanuri, Fulani and Nupe also caution against a single northern label. Their histories, languages and relations to the emirate order differed, even where Islam influenced courts and kingship. To call them all theocratic before checking the evidence is to replace three different arrangements with a convenient slogan. The examiner uses the Tiv precisely to punish that shortcut.

The same caution applies to the south. Yoruba monarchy and Igbo acephalous consensus look like opposites, but both contained checks: councils and cults checked an Oba, while elders, age grades and title societies checked the assembly. Focusing only on the presence or absence of a throne misses the shared concern with limiting a single will.

Understanding that variation protects against a common trap. A question that asks about a non-centralised group in the north does not expect the emirate answer, and a question about the Igbo does not expect a council of nobles. Locate each people in its own arrangement first; only then compare them.
bullets: The Tiv break the northern emirate pattern and show its limits.
Kanuri, Nupe and Fulani arrangements should not be merged without evidence.
Both Yoruba and Igbo systems checked power, but through different bodies.
Name the arrangement before comparing it with another.

lessons.title: Political Parties and Party Systems
lessons.objective: Explain what parties do, how they are organised, and how one-party, two-party, multi-party and dominant-party systems differ.

content.heading: Parties in one sentence
paragraphs: A political party is an organised group that seeks to win elections and control government.

content.heading: What a party is for
paragraphs: A group of professionals registers a party, opens a ward office and publishes a manifesto before the primaries. That combination of organisation, programme and ambition to govern is what separates a party from a discussion club.

A party has a formal name, a membership roll and a constitution. It is organised from the ward through the local government and state to the national convention, which is its highest decision-making body, while the national executive committee runs it between conventions.
Its functions are to aggregate interests, recruit and train leaders, turn its manifesto into policy, mobilise voters, organise government after victory and scrutinise the government when it loses.
bullets: Ward → local government → state → national.
Manifesto: what the party would do in office.
Aggregate, recruit, formulate, mobilise, govern, oppose.
content.takeaway: A party is judged by whether it can turn many interests into one programme and then govern.

check.question: A political party can be said to have a national outlook if ______.
options: it is ethnic-based but has branches across the country
it is registered by the electoral commission as a national party
it is led by people who are famous at home and abroad
its membership cuts across ethnic boundaries
check.why: A national outlook is about the spread of membership and leadership, not the number of branches or the fact of registration.

content.heading: Party systems
paragraphs: In one election two parties take almost every seat. In another, six parties enter parliament and three of them form a coalition. The difference is the party system, not the number of parties registered.

A one-party system allows only one legal or effective party and offers stability without choice. A two-party system lets two parties alternate in power, as Nigeria's First Republic did with the NPC and NCNC, and as the PDP and APC have done since 2015.

A multi-party system lets several parties compete and usually govern through coalitions, which represents more views but can be unstable. A dominant-party system is competitive in law yet one party wins repeatedly, as the NPN did from 1979 to 1983 and the PDP from 1999 to 2015.
bullets: One-party: no choice. Two-party: alternation.
Multi-party: coalitions. Dominant-party: repeated wins.
Nigeria 2015: the first opposition victory at federal level.
content.takeaway: The number of parties matters less than whether power can actually change hands.

check.question: A party system in which several parties compete but one wins every election is best described as ______.
check.why: Other parties are legal and contest, but one party's repeated victory makes the system dominant-party rather than multi-party in practice.

content.heading: Organisation, candidates and money
paragraphs: A national chairman overrules a state chapter's choice of candidate, and the loser defects to another party. Both incidents show that party organisation and candidate selection decide who reaches the ballot.

Candidates are chosen through primaries, direct or indirect, and the national executive can sometimes impose a candidate. Internal democracy is weak when a few leaders control the list, and defections follow.
Parties are financed by dues, levies, donations and, in some countries, public funds. Without disclosure, wealthy sponsors can capture the party and its manifesto.
bullets: Primaries: direct or indirect.
Finance: dues, levies, donations, public funds.
Weak internal democracy produces defections.
content.takeaway: Party organisation decides who gets on the ballot; party finance decides who can afford to.

check.question: The party body that runs the party between national conventions is the ______.
check.why: The convention is supreme but meets occasionally; the national executive committee carries on the day-to-day work between conventions.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Registration does not make a party national. A national outlook means membership and leadership cut across ethnic and regional lines, not merely branches in every state.

content.problem: Classify each case: (a) only one party is legal; (b) two parties alternate in power; (c) five parties win seats and three form a coalition; (d) one party wins every election while others compete.

steps.reason: Only one legal party means there is no electoral choice.
steps.predictPrompt: What happens when two parties alternate?

steps.reason: Two parties taking turns in government is the defining feature of a two-party system.
steps.predictPrompt: What would a weaker answer look like here?

steps.reason: Several parties winning seats and forming coalitions is multi-party; repeated victory by one competitor is dominant-party.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.question: Why is a national outlook about membership rather than the number of branch offices, and what does that imply for a party that wants to win a national majority?
hints: Branches can exist in every state while leadership and membership stay tied to one ethnic or regional group.
A national party must aggregate interests from many groups, not merely represent one.
Link ethnic breadth to winning a national majority and to legitimacy after victory.

content.heading: Go deeper: How party systems shape stability and representation
paragraphs: A party system is not a register of parties. It describes the pattern of competition that results from how many effective parties exist and whether elections can change the government. A state with dozens of registered parties may still have a stable two-party contest, while a state with only a few parties may offer no genuine choice if the same party always wins.

Two-party systems reward convergence. With only two serious contenders, each must appeal to the median voter, so governments tend to be moderate and alternation is clear. That clarity brings stability, but it can also crowd out minority interests. Nigeria showed the alternation logic in the First Republic contest between the NPC and NCNC, and again when the PDP and the APC contested national power from 2015.

Multi-party systems reward breadth. Several parties can enter the legislature, minority views can survive, and governments often depend on coalitions. Representation improves, but coalition bargaining can make policy slow and difficult for voters to reward or punish. A coalition that no single party controls is harder to hold responsible than a government of one party.

Dominant-party systems sit between competition and closure. Other parties are legal and campaign, yet one party wins repeatedly because it controls resources, patronage or the grievances of others. The NPN period from 1979 to 1983 and the PDP era from 1999 to 2015 fit that description. Stability is real, but it is purchased by weakening the expectation that a loss is possible.
bullets: A system describes effective competition and whether power can change hands.
Two-party systems favour moderation and clear alternation.
Multi-party systems favour representation but depend on coalitions.
Dominant-party systems allow rivals while delaying turnover.

content.heading: Go deeper: Primaries, imposition and the quiet collapse of discipline
paragraphs: Getting on the ballot often matters more than getting elected, because a primary decides who carries the party label into the general contest. Direct primaries ask members to choose, indirect primaries ask delegates, and imposition removes the choice from voters in the ward or constituency. The label stays the same, but the degree of internal democracy behind it changes completely.

National machinery can overturn local choices. The national convention is the supreme body when it meets, while the national executive committee runs the party between conventions. If state chapters, ward executives and national officers disagree, the public sees factions rather than one membership. Losers who believe the process was rigged often defect to a rival party, carrying their structures with them.

Finance deepens the distortion. Dues and levies spread cost widely, while large donations concentrate influence in sponsors who can fund campaigns, offices and litigation. Without disclosure and limits, candidates begin to answer to financiers rather than members. Public funding, where it exists, can reduce that dependence but creates a new question about who decides the rate and the recipients.

Discipline is therefore not a slogan. It is the outcome of fair primaries, predictable conventions, honest registers and finance that members can inspect. A party that selects candidates by favour and pays for organisation through a few hands should expect defections, because excluded aspirants have no reason to remain loyal to a label that gave them no chance.
bullets: Direct, indirect and imposed selection produce different levels of internal democracy.
National convention is supreme; the national executive committee runs daily affairs.
Large donations can shift loyalty from members to sponsors.
Defection usually follows unfair selection rather than preceding it.

content.heading: Go deeper: National outlook is about people, not branch offices
paragraphs: A party can open offices in every state and still remain regional in spirit. Branch offices prove logistics, not belonging. The national question concerns where members come from, where leaders are drawn from and which interests the manifesto must satisfy. A party of one ethnic or regional group has not solved that problem by renting in the capital.

Aggregation tests the claim. Parties must combine farmers and traders, workers and professionals, religious groups and regions into a programme broad enough for a national majority. An aggregating convention debates policy and balances tickets across groups. Without that combination, a party may dominate one region and lack votes and legitimacy for the federation.

Nigeria makes the test strict. The Independent National Electoral Commission registers parties under constitutional conditions, and national ambition requires campaigning across federal and state tiers. A state party may be effective locally, but without alliances it cannot command a federal majority. The federation punishes purely local appeal nationally.

The exam trap reverses the logic. It offers branches, registration, famous leaders or an imposing headquarters as proof. None proves that membership and leadership cut across ethnic and regional lines. One group's support under many office signs is a regional party with national offices.
bullets: Branch offices prove organisation, not national outlook.
Aggregation combines many interests into one programme.
Federal majorities need support beyond one base.
Registration and famous leaders do not prove national membership.

lessons.title: Foreign Policy: Goals and Instruments
lessons.objective: Explain what foreign policy is, Nigeria's Afrocentric goals and principles, the instruments states use, and the cases that show them.

content.heading: Foreign policy in one sentence
paragraphs: Foreign policy is a state's strategy for dealing with other states and international organisations.

content.heading: What foreign policy is
paragraphs: A boundary dispute with a neighbour moves from a local skirmish to a case at the International Court of Justice. How a state handles that dispute, and every other dealing beyond its borders, is its foreign policy.

Foreign policy is the set of goals and methods a state uses in its relations with other states and international organisations. Its objectives are usually security, economic advantage, national prestige and the promotion of an ideology or values.

The instruments are diplomacy, trade, foreign aid, military force, propaganda and membership of multilateral bodies. Geography, history, the economy, domestic politics and the character of leaders all shape which instruments a state reaches for.
bullets: Goals: security, economy, prestige, values.
Instruments: diplomacy, trade, aid, force, multilateralism.
Determinants: geography, history, economy, politics, leadership.
content.takeaway: Foreign policy is domestic policy continued abroad, with fewer courts to enforce it.

check.question: Which of these is an instrument rather than an objective of foreign policy?
check.why: Diplomacy is a method a state uses; security, economic advantage and prestige are goals it pursues.

content.heading: Nigeria's Afrocentric goals
paragraphs: At independence in 1960 Nigeria declared itself Afrocentric, but Balewa's government was cautious: it opposed apartheid and supported decolonisation without breaking with Britain.

The goals were to defend sovereignty and territory, promote African decolonisation and unity, support peace and security, and pursue economic development. The principles were Afrocentrism, non-alignment, sovereign equality, non-interference and peaceful settlement of disputes.

The Murtala/Obasanjo regime reviewed foreign policy from 1975 and made it more assertive against apartheid and white minority rule. The review was conducted by the Adedeji Commission, and later governments added economic diplomacy to the older political goals.
bullets: Afrocentrism: Africa at the centre.
Principles: non-alignment, equality, non-interference.
1975 review: Adedeji Commission under Murtala/Obasanjo.
content.takeaway: Nigeria's foreign policy has been Afrocentric in rhetoric and pragmatic about where the money comes from.

check.question: The basis of Nigeria's foreign policy during the Independence Constitution era was ______.
check.why: Afrocentrism was declared at independence; anti-apartheid was one part of it, and the other options misdescribe the declared basis.

content.heading: Instruments and cases
paragraphs: Nigeria took the Bakassi Peninsula dispute with Cameroon to the International Court of Justice, which ruled in 2002, and the Greentree Agreement of 2006 implemented the handover.

In 1986 Nigeria withdrew from the Edinburgh Commonwealth Games to protest Britain's failure to impose sanctions on apartheid South Africa. Both cases show the same instruments: law where it can bind, and symbolic withdrawal where it cannot.
Nigeria also uses peacekeeping, as with ECOMOG in Liberia and Sierra Leone, and aid to African states. Military force is the last instrument, because it is costly and invites retaliation.
bullets: Bakassi: ICJ 2002, Greentree 2006.
Edinburgh 1986: protest at Britain over apartheid.
Peacekeeping: ECOMOG in Liberia and Sierra Leone.
content.takeaway: Law and symbolism are instruments too; a state uses the cheapest one that can work.

check.question: Nigeria's withdrawal from the Edinburgh Commonwealth Games in July 1986 was in protest against British ______.
options: support for UNITA rebels in Angola
failure to impose sanctions on South Africa's apartheid government
check.why: The boycott was over Britain's refusal to sanction apartheid South Africa, not over arms, words or Angola.

visual.caption: Nigeria's foreign policy moved from cautious Afrocentrism to assertion and then economic diplomacy.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Afrocentrism is the centre of gravity, not a promise to ignore other interests. Nigeria traded with Britain and later courted investors while insisting on African liberation.

content.problem: Classify each instrument: (a) Nigeria sues Cameroon at the ICJ over Bakassi; (b) Nigeria withdraws from the Edinburgh Games; (c) Nigeria sends troops to ECOMOG in Liberia; (d) Nigeria gives aid to a drought-hit African state.

steps.reason: A court case uses legal settlement; a Games boycott uses symbolic withdrawal.
steps.predictPrompt: What kind of instrument is a peacekeeping deployment?

steps.reason: Sending troops under a regional mandate is a military and peacekeeping instrument.
steps.predictPrompt: What would a weaker answer look like here?

steps.reason: Aid is an economic instrument intended to build influence and goodwill.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?
