content.question: Why did a militarily weaker Nigeria rely on law and symbolism against stronger states, and when would military force have been the wrong instrument?
hints: The ICJ gave Nigeria a binding forum it could not get through force.
A Games boycott cost little but spoke to the Commonwealth and to domestic opinion.
Military force is costly, invites retaliation and needs regional or international cover.

content.heading: Go deeper: Non-alignment from the weak side of the table
paragraphs: Non-alignment is not silence or agreement with everyone. It is a strategy for states that cannot defend themselves alone: refuse rival blocs, keep alliances temporary and use organisations to turn legal equality into influence. A small delegation still counts as one vote in a general assembly, and a treaty still binds a powerful neighbour.

Sovereign equality gives that strategy its footing. Each state is legally equal regardless of population or wealth, so a bloc of African votes can shape the agenda of the United Nations or the African Union in a way no single state could. Non-interference protects the same point: stronger powers may persuade, but cannot decide domestic matters without breaking the norm.

Peaceful settlement is the working method. Courts, mediation and peacekeeping mandates give Nigeria a forum where Cameroon, a rebel movement or a distant sponsor must at least answer. The process creates a record, attracts support and raises the cost of force. For a middle power, talk is not empty when the alternative is an unsustainable war.

Neighbourhood comes first. Geography places Nigeria among states with porous borders, shared ties and competing resources. ECOWAS and border settlements decide whether news arrives as a diplomatic note or as a raid. A strategy that works in a distant capital but fails on the border has missed its purpose.
bullets: Non-alignment keeps alliances temporary and preserves a free vote.
Sovereign equality turns many weak votes into influence.
International forums raise the cost of force.
Neighbourhood security is tested first on Nigeria’s borders.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why law, protest and peacekeeping suited Nigeria’s position
paragraphs: Nigeria could not fight every dispute it cared about, so it chose instruments whose cost matched its power. Taking Bakassi to the International Court of Justice placed the case where maps, treaties and argument mattered more than army size. The Court ruled in 2002 and the Greentree Agreement of 2006 carried out the handover.

The Edinburgh withdrawal in 1986 used a different economy of power. Leaving the Commonwealth Games did not move a border or impose a sanction, but it denied Britain a celebration and publicised Nigeria’s anger at Britain’s refusal to impose sanctions on apartheid South Africa. A boycott is cheap, visible and reversible.

Peacekeeping through ECOMOG in Liberia and Sierra Leone reversed the voice. Nigeria supplied troops, money and command, and showed neighbours it could protect order as well as demand it. That role bought prestige and a reputation for regional responsibility, while exposing soldiers to danger and budgets to heavy costs.

Together the cases teach one choice. Use law where a court can bind, use symbolism where only opinion can move, and use soldiers only where regional cover and a clear mandate make the expense defensible. Each instrument carries a different bill.
bullets: The ICJ and Greentree turned Bakassi into law and transfer.
Edinburgh 1986 traded a cheap boycott for public shame.
ECOMOG converted troops into regional prestige at real cost.
Choose the cheapest instrument that can bind or persuade.

content.heading: Go deeper: From political Afrocentrism to economic diplomacy
paragraphs: Nigeria declared itself Afrocentric at independence in 1960, yet the Balewa government still protected trade and security links with Britain. That caution was not hypocrisy; it reflected an economy that needed markets, investors and manufactured goods. A new state can proclaim African solidarity while depending on the very partners whose colonial ties it criticises, and the tension shapes every decision.

The review of 1975 under the Murtala/Obasanjo regime, conducted by the Adedeji Commission, pushed the balance toward assertion. Nigeria opposed apartheid and white minority rule more openly and treated African liberation as a central test of respect. The shift was political before it was economic, because the immediate aim was to prove that an African state could set its own agenda without seeking permission from former colonial powers.

Economic diplomacy, prominent after 1999, added a second ledger. Trade, investment, energy sales and technology now compete with liberation rhetoric. A government that needs foreign capital cannot easily threaten the investors it courts, while a government that ignores liberation loses the African leadership it claims. The result is not a choice between principle and interest but a constant negotiation between them.

Domestic politics decides how that negotiation sounds. A leader who needs votes at home may speak firmly abroad, while the same leader in a capital of investors may speak softly. Foreign policy is therefore domestic policy continued with weaker enforcement: budgets, elections and public anger at home all limit what a president can promise or threaten thousands of miles away.
bullets: Afrocentrism coexisted with dependence on British trade after 1960.
The 1975 Adedeji review made opposition to white minority rule more assertive.
Economic diplomacy after 1999 balanced liberation against investment.
Domestic budgets and elections narrow what leaders can promise abroad.

lessons.title: Citizenship: Acquisition, Rights and Loss
lessons.objective: Differentiate the routes to citizenship, separate rights from duties, state what the state owes, and explain dual citizenship, renunciation and deprivation.

content.heading: Citizenship in one sentence
paragraphs: Citizenship is the legal bond between a person and a state, and it carries rights, duties and protection that residence alone never creates.

content.heading: A girl born in Lagos, a woman married in Kano
paragraphs: A girl is born in Lagos to parents from Enugu, and a woman marries a Nigerian in Kano; both are citizens. A trader from Chad has lived in Nigeria for twenty years, yet he remains an alien, because citizenship follows law rather than length of stay.

Section 25 grants citizenship by birth: born in Nigeria before independence to a parent or grandparent from an indigenous community, or born in Nigeria after independence to a citizen parent or grandparent. The fourth route, descent, covers a person born outside Nigeria to a citizen parent.
Registration covers a woman married to a citizen; naturalisation covers an adult foreigner of good character who has lived in Nigeria for fifteen years and takes the oath of allegiance.
bullets: Birth: born in Nigeria to a citizen parent or grandparent.
Descent: born abroad to a citizen parent.
Registration for marriage; naturalisation after fifteen years.
content.takeaway: Citizenship is acquired by law, not by residence or property.

check.question: A man born in Ghana to Nigerian parents has never lived in Nigeria. His status is ______.
options: a citizen only after fifteen years
check.why: A person born outside Nigeria to a citizen parent is a citizen by descent; residence is irrelevant.

content.heading: The right to speak, the duty to pay
paragraphs: A trader criticises a governor on radio, then pays his market levy. The criticism is protected by Chapter IV of the Constitution; the levy is a duty under section 24.

Chapter IV rights include life, dignity, personal liberty, fair hearing, private and family life, thought and conscience, expression, peaceful assembly, movement, property and freedom from discrimination. They bind government and can be enforced in court.

Section 24 duties are to respect the Constitution and national symbols, respect other people's rights, assist lawful agencies, pay taxes and defend Nigeria when required. The state must also protect rights and pursue welfare and security under Chapter II, though those goals are not directly enforceable.
bullets: Rights are claims the citizen can enforce against the state.
Duties are obligations owed to the state and to other citizens.
Freedom of conscience is a right, not a civil obligation.
content.takeaway: Rights protect the person; duties protect the state and other citizens.

check.question: Which of these is a duty of a Nigerian citizen?
check.why: Paying tax is a section 24 duty; conscience, fair hearing and movement are Chapter IV rights.

content.heading: A Canadian passport, a renunciation
paragraphs: A naturalised citizen acquires Canadian citizenship and loses Nigerian citizenship; a citizen by birth who does the same keeps it. Section 28 protects dual citizenship for citizens by birth; a new nationality ends the other routes.

Renunciation is voluntary: a citizen of full age declares that he or she is giving up the status, and the President registers the declaration, though he may refuse during a war. Deprivation is imposed by the state, mainly for disloyalty, trading with the enemy, or a long prison sentence soon after naturalisation.

The state's side is protection: security at home, consular help abroad, and welfare, education and health under Chapter II. A person who loses citizenship loses its rights, though many Chapter IV rights protect everyone in Nigeria.
bullets: Birth citizenship allows a second passport.
A new nationality ends citizenship by registration or naturalisation.
Renunciation is voluntary; deprivation is imposed for disloyalty or crime.
content.takeaway: Birth citizenship survives a second passport; registration and naturalisation do not.

check.question: A Nigerian who became a citizen by registration takes the citizenship of another country. What happens?
options: Citizenship is suspended for five years
check.why: Section 28: voluntarily taking a new nationality ends citizenship by registration or naturalisation, not birth.

visual.caption: Both end citizenship, but renunciation is the citizen's choice and deprivation is the state's decision.

rows.left: The citizen no longer wants the status
rows.right: Disloyalty, enemy trade or a long prison term

rows.left: Did the citizen choose to give it up?

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Property, residence and marriage do not by themselves make a citizen. Marriage opens registration; fifteen years' residence opens naturalisation; buying land opens nothing. Read the stem closely too: a civil obligation is a duty, so an option naming a right such as freedom of conscience is the exception.

content.problem: Classify each person: (a) a child born in Ibadan to parents from Ogun State; (b) a Lebanese trader born in Beirut who has lived in Kano for sixteen years and takes the oath; (c) a Nigerian-born engineer who also holds a British passport.

steps.reason: Birth in Nigeria to citizen parents is citizenship by birth under section 25.
steps.predictPrompt: Does residence alone ever confer citizenship?

steps.reason: Sixteen years' residence, good character and the oath meet the naturalisation conditions.
steps.predictPrompt: In your own words, why does this step come before the next one?

steps.reason: A citizen by birth may hold another citizenship without losing Nigerian citizenship.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.question: A Nigerian citizen by birth takes a British passport. A naturalised Nigerian does the same. Explain what happens to each, and name one duty each still owes while a citizen.
hints: Section 28 permits dual citizenship for citizens by birth.
Registration and naturalisation end when another citizenship is voluntarily acquired.
Duties continue while citizenship lasts: obey the law, pay tax, respect national symbols, defend the country.

content.heading: Go deeper: The sections that decide citizenship
paragraphs: Chapter III of the 1999 Constitution is short but precise. Section 25 defines citizenship by birth; section 26 provides registration, chiefly for a woman married to a citizen and for a person of full age born outside Nigeria any of whose grandparents is a citizen; section 27 sets naturalisation. Sections 28 to 30 deal with dual citizenship, renunciation and deprivation.

Naturalisation is not a formality. The applicant must be of full age and capacity, of good character, intend to be domiciled in Nigeria, be acceptable to the local community, be capable of contributing to national development, take the oath and show fifteen years' continuous residence or fifteen years in the aggregate over the preceding twenty. The President grants the certificate.

The rules are not gender-neutral. A foreign woman married to a Nigerian may register, while a foreign husband must naturalise, and the 1999 text makes no provision for foundlings or adopted children to acquire citizenship. Statelessness monitors have criticised both gaps.

Renunciation is the citizen's own act under section 29: an adult declares the intention, and the President registers it, though registration may be refused during a war or where it is contrary to public policy.

Section 28 withdraws citizenship from a registered or naturalised citizen who acquires or keeps a nationality of which he is not a citizen by birth, and section 30 allows deprivation for disloyalty, trading with the enemy, or a prison sentence of three years or more within seven years of naturalisation. A citizen by birth keeps Nigerian citizenship after taking a second passport.
bullets: Sections 25 to 27 create the routes; 28 to 30 regulate dual status, renunciation and deprivation.
Naturalisation needs fifteen years' residence, good character, the oath and a contribution to development.
Foreign wives register; foreign husbands naturalise, an asymmetry critics want removed.

content.heading: Go deeper: Dual citizenship and public office
paragraphs: Dual citizenship is lawful in Nigeria, but not for everyone on the same terms. A citizen by birth may hold another nationality and travel on either passport; a citizen by registration or naturalisation cannot, because voluntary acquisition of another nationality ends the Nigerian status.

Public office sharpens the question. The President and state governors must be citizens by birth under sections 131 and 177, so a naturalised citizen cannot contest those offices even after decades of service. For other offices the Constitution requires citizenship, and election petitions have turned on whether a candidate lost it.

The practical trap is documentary. A candidate who naturalised abroad, or who renounced Nigerian citizenship and later reacquired it by registration, may satisfy the age and party tests yet fail the citizenship test. Read the constitutional text, not the passport in hand.

Dual citizenship also affects duties. A citizen abroad still owes allegiance, may be called to defend Nigeria, and remains liable to tax on Nigerian-source income. A second passport does not switch off section 24.
bullets: Birth citizens may hold a second passport; registered and naturalised citizens may not.
The President and governors must be citizens by birth.
A second passport does not cancel the duties of citizenship.

content.heading: Go deeper: What the state owes the citizen
paragraphs: The syllabus asks you to assess the obligations of the state, and the Constitution splits them in two. Chapter IV rights, from life and fair hearing to expression, movement and property, are enforceable: a citizen can sue a public officer who violates them. Chapter II duties, covering security, welfare, education and health, are directive principles that guide government but are not directly enforceable.

That distinction explains why an underfunded school rarely produces a successful lawsuit, while a detention without trial can be challenged at once. Section 14(2) still declares that the security and welfare of the people shall be the primary purpose of government, but section 6(6)(c) keeps Chapter II out of the courts.

Abroad, the state owes diplomatic and consular protection. A Nigerian arrested in another country can ask the embassy for help, though the embassy cannot override that country's courts. At home, the police and armed forces carry the duty to protect life and property, and their failure can ground a claim in damages.

The bargain is unequal but real: the citizen pays tax, obeys the law and may be conscripted; the state protects rights, provides security and pursues welfare. Exams reward the student who can say which side is enforceable.
bullets: Chapter IV rights are enforceable; Chapter II goals are not directly justiciable.
Section 14(2) makes security and welfare the primary purpose of government.
Consular protection abroad is part of the state's duty, but it cannot overturn foreign courts.

lessons.title: Political Ideologies: From Communalism to Fascism
lessons.objective: Define ideology, contrast the modes of production, and distinguish capitalism, socialism, communism, liberalism, conservatism, totalitarianism, fascism and nazism.

content.heading: Ideology in one sentence
paragraphs: An ideology is an organised set of beliefs about who should own wealth, how production should be run, and how much liberty the state should allow.

content.heading: From shared land to wage labour
paragraphs: In a communal village, land belongs to the lineage and every household works it; under feudalism, a noble holds the land and peasants owe labour and military service; in a factory, a private owner buys labour and sells the product. Each is a mode of production, and the difference is who owns what and who works for whom.

Communalism is the earliest form: common ownership, shared work and no separate ruling class. Feudalism ties land to service, producing lords and serfs. Capitalism separates owners of capital from wage earners and organises production for profit in a market.
bullets: Communalism: common land, shared work, no classes.
Feudalism: noble-owned land worked by peasants for service.
Capitalism: private capital, wage labour, production for profit.
content.takeaway: Modes of production differ in who owns the land, tools and labour.

check.question: In which mode of production do peasants work land granted by a noble in return for labour and military service?
check.why: Land held by a noble and worked for service is the feudal relationship; capitalism pays wages instead.

content.heading: Who owns the steel mill?
paragraphs: A steel mill can be owned by shareholders who seek profit, by the state which sets output targets, or by the community in common. The first is capitalism, the second socialism, the third the communist ideal.

Capitalism rests on private ownership of the means of production, market prices and the profit motive. Socialism places the means of production under social or state ownership and uses planning to reduce inequality, but it usually keeps elections and some private property.

Communism, in Marxist theory, aims at common ownership and a classless society in which the state eventually withers away. Marxism calls this the end of class struggle; the practical test is ownership plus who decides what is produced.
bullets: Capitalism: private owners, markets, profit.
Socialism: social or state ownership, planning, equality.
Communism: common ownership, classless society, stateless end point.
content.takeaway: Ownership and who plans production separate the three.

check.question: Which statement separates communism from socialism?
options: Communism accepts private ownership of heavy industry
Communism aims at a classless and eventually stateless society
Socialism is driven by the profit motive
check.why: Socialism keeps the state and some private property; communism aims at common ownership and a classless, stateless society.

visual.caption: Capitalism and socialism answer the ownership question differently, and that difference drives the rest.

content.heading: A free press, an old constitution, a silenced nation
paragraphs: A liberal wants a smaller prison budget and a free press; a conservative wants the old constitution kept; a fascist wants the nation armed and the individual silenced. The labels describe attitudes to liberty, tradition and state power.

Liberalism stresses individual liberty, consent, limited government and gradual reform. Conservatism stresses tradition, order and inherited institutions, and distrusts rapid change. Totalitarianism goes further than either: one party controls political, economic and private life through censorship and terror.

Fascism is totalitarian and ultranationalist, with a single leader, glorified force and the individual subordinated to the nation. Nazism adds a racial hierarchy and expansionist war to that fascist core. Imperialism is expansion abroad; Lewis Samuel called pure conquest and exploitation regressive imperialism.
bullets: Liberalism: liberty and reform; conservatism: tradition and order.
Totalitarianism controls everything; fascism adds ultranationalism and force.
Nazism adds racial doctrine; regressive imperialism is conquest for its own sake.
content.takeaway: Liberty, tradition and total control sort the modern ideologies.

check.question: Which ideology combines total state control with a doctrine of racial superiority?
check.why: Nazism is the fascist state plus a racial hierarchy; fascism alone is ultranationalist and totalitarian.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Do not merge socialism and communism: socialism usually allows private property and elections, while communism envisages common ownership and a classless, stateless society. Do not merge fascism and nazism either: nazism adds racial doctrine to the fascist state.

content.problem: Name the ideology behind each statement: (a) “land belongs to the lineage and is worked in common”; (b) “the state should own the banks and plan output”; (c) “the nation is supreme and the leader rules by force”.

steps.reason: Common ownership by the lineage, with no noble or private owner, is communalism.
steps.predictPrompt: Which statement gives the state the banks?

steps.reason: State ownership plus planning is the socialist position.
steps.predictPrompt: What does the question tell you to find first?

steps.reason: Ultranationalism, a single leader and rule by force are fascist.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test this answer before writing it down?

content.question: A new party promises free markets, low taxes and private ownership. Which ideology does it draw on, and how would a socialist answer its claim that private ownership is efficient?
hints: Free markets and private ownership point to capitalism or liberalism.
The socialist answer stresses inequality, public goods and planning.
A strong answer names the ideology and weighs efficiency against equality.

content.heading: Go deeper: Modes of production from communalism to capitalism
paragraphs: Communalism describes societies in which land and tools belong to the lineage or community and production is mainly for use. Many pre-colonial Nigerian communities held land this way, with the family or village allocating plots; communal tenure did not mean equality, since elders and men usually controlled allocation.

Feudalism organised land through a hierarchy of lords and vassals. The lord held the land, the peasant worked it, and the rent was paid in labour, produce or military service. The system tied people to land and made wealth a matter of status rather than market price.

Capitalism emerged when land, labour and money became commodities. Enclosure pushed peasants off the land, factories gathered workers under one roof, and the owner sold the product at a profit. Colonial rule pulled Nigerian agriculture and trade into this market system, though communal tenure survived in many areas.

The mode-of-production question is therefore not just who is rich. It asks who owns the means of production, who works them, and how the surplus is divided. That is why the syllabus pairs ideology with modes of production.
bullets: Communal tenure: lineage or village ownership, production for use.
Feudal tenure: land for service, wealth tied to status.
Capitalist tenure: private ownership, wage labour, production for profit.

content.heading: Go deeper: Socialism, communism and the Nigerian mixed economy
paragraphs: Marx and Engels argued in the Communist Manifesto that capitalism creates its own gravediggers: wage labour, competition and crisis would push workers towards collective ownership. Their communism envisaged a classless society and the withering away of the state, with a transitional workers' state in between.

Lenin adapted that theory to a vanguard party and used it to justify the Bolshevik revolution of 1917. Social democrats took a different road, accepting elections, markets and a welfare state while taxing and regulating capitalism. The Nordic model is the best-known version.

Nigeria has a mixed economy. The state owns or regulates oil, power and other strategic sectors, while markets dominate agriculture, trade and services. Privatisation since 1999 has sold many public enterprises, but the state still owns the national oil company and regulates the sector.

Nigerian parties rarely divide along ideology. Campaigns turn on personality, patronage and ethnic or regional balance, and parties often adopt the same market-friendly language. That is why exam questions ask you to recognise an ideology from its principles rather than from a party label.
bullets: Marxism predicts common ownership and a stateless, classless end point.
Social democracy accepts markets and elections but redistributes through the state.
Nigeria runs a mixed economy, and its parties are weakly ideological.

content.heading: Go deeper: Totalitarianism, fascism and nazism
paragraphs: Totalitarianism is a twentieth-century concept, associated with Hannah Arendt's study of Nazi Germany and Stalinist Russia. It describes a system with one party, an official ideology, a secret police, a monopoly of communications and weapons, and a centralised economy. The state claims control over private life as well as public life.

Fascism began in Italy under Mussolini, who marched on Rome in 1922. It glorified the nation and the will of the leader, organised the economy into corporations, and treated violence and war as virtues. It was totalitarian in ambition but kept the monarchy and the church as partners.

Nazism was the German variant. It kept the fascist leader cult and terror, then added a racial hierarchy, antisemitism and a demand for living space in eastern Europe. That racial doctrine is the line examiners draw between fascism and nazism.

These labels are not interchangeable with authoritarianism. An authoritarian regime limits political competition but leaves room for private life and some pluralism; a totalitarian one tries to abolish that room altogether.
bullets: Totalitarianism: one party, one ideology, terror and control of private life.
Fascism: ultranationalism, leader cult, corporatism and glorified force.
Nazism: fascism plus racial hierarchy and expansionist war.

lessons.title: Structures of Governance: Unitary, Federal and Confederal
lessons.objective: Compare unitary, federal and confederal structures, explain why each is adopted, and give its merits and demerits.

content.heading: Structure in one sentence
paragraphs: A structure of government describes how power is shared between the centre and the regions, not who holds the top office.

content.heading: One parliament, one police force
paragraphs: A teacher in Sokoto and a teacher in Port Harcourt are paid from the same national payroll under the same curriculum, because one parliament and one ministry set the rule for the whole country. That is a unitary structure.

In a unitary state the central government holds all legal power. It may create local councils and give them duties, but it can also abolish them, because their powers come from an ordinary law and not from the constitution. There is one constitution, one citizenship and usually one police force.

Its merits are uniform standards, cheaper administration and quick decisions. Its demerits are an overloaded centre, neglect of local needs, and the risk that a single national government becomes remote or tyrannical. Britain, France, Ghana and Japan are unitary; Nigeria was unitary before the 1946 Richards Constitution.
bullets: One constitution, one citizenship, one centre.
Local councils exist at the centre's pleasure.
Examples: Britain, France, Ghana.
content.takeaway: In a unitary state the centre can reorganise the local tier at will.

check.question: Which feature marks a unitary state?
options: Local councils have constitutionally protected powers
The centre may abolish local councils by ordinary law
Two levels of government are coordinate
check.why: In a unitary state local councils are created by statute, so the centre can also abolish them; protected units are the federal marker.

content.heading: Two governments, each with its own sphere
paragraphs: A state government builds a feeder road while the federal government builds the expressway, each from its own budget and its own legal power. Neither can abolish the other, because the constitution divides power between them. That is a federation.

A federal state has two levels of government, each coordinate and independent within its sphere. A written constitution lists what each may do, a supreme court settles disputes, and the units have their own legislatures. Nigeria divides power into exclusive, concurrent and residual lists, and federal law prevails where the two conflict on concurrent matters.

Federalism is adopted in large or diverse countries to hold different peoples together without smothering them. Its merits are local autonomy and a check on central power; its demerits are costly duplication, revenue and boundary disputes, and slow decisions.
Nigeria, the United States, India and Canada are federal.
bullets: Power divided by a written constitution.
Neither level can abolish the other.
Examples: Nigeria, the United States, India.
content.takeaway: A federation is a bargain the centre cannot cancel on its own.

check.question: What makes a division of power federal rather than merely decentralised?
options: Local councils are created by statute
The constitution protects the lower tier's powers
The centre may dissolve state assemblies
check.why: Constitutional protection is the federal test; a centre that can abolish or appoint the units is still unitary.

visual.caption: The test is not how many tiers exist but whether the constitution protects the lower tier's power.

content.heading: A centre that cannot command
paragraphs: A league of states opens a joint secretariat for defence and trade, but each member keeps its own army, currency and veto, and may leave at will. The secretariat can propose, not command. That is a confederation.

A confederation is a union of sovereign states that delegate a few powers to a weak central body. Decisions need unanimity, citizens owe their main allegiance to their own state, and the right of withdrawal is real. It is adopted to secure common defence or trade without surrendering independence.

Its merit is that it protects each state's independence and makes cooperation voluntary. Its demerits are weakness in war and economic policy, slow decisions and easy collapse. The Articles of Confederation and the Swiss union before 1848 are the standard examples.
A confederation is a structure, not a system: it says how centre and units share power, not how the executive meets the legislature.
bullets: Sovereign units, weak centre, right of withdrawal.
Decisions need agreement, not command.
content.takeaway: A confederation is a treaty among states, not a government over them.

check.question: Which statement describes a confederation?
options: The units keep sovereign powers and may withdraw
The centre may abolish the units
One parliament legislates for all the units
The centre appoints the unit governors
check.why: Sovereign units with a right of withdrawal are the confederal marker; the other options describe a unitary or federal centre.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Form asks who rules; system asks how the executive and legislature relate; structure asks how the centre and the units share power. Nigeria is a federal republic with a presidential system.

content.problem: Classify each case: (a) Britain, where Parliament at Westminster can abolish any local council; (b) Nigeria, where the constitution lists federal and state powers; (c) the American league of 1781, where each state kept its sovereignty.

steps.reason: A centre that can abolish local councils by ordinary law holds all legal power.
steps.predictPrompt: Which case has a constitutionally protected lower tier?

steps.reason: Two levels are coordinate and the constitution divides power between them.
steps.predictPrompt: What would a weaker answer look like here?

steps.reason: Sovereign states delegating a few powers to a weak centre form a confederation.

content.question: Nigeria has 36 states and 774 local government areas, yet it is called a federation with a strong centre. Explain two features that make it federal and one that pulls power to the centre.
hints: Federal features: a written constitution, coordinate levels, a supreme court, state legislatures.
Centralising features: oil revenue and the Federation Account, federal roads and police, military-era decrees.
A strong answer pairs each feature with the effect it has on state autonomy.

content.heading: Go deeper: Federal, decentralised or merely busy at the centre
paragraphs: Many states have local councils, regional offices and national ministries without being federal. The question is not how many tiers exist but who can abolish whom. In a decentralised unitary state the centre creates local bodies by ordinary law and can reorganise or abolish them at will. In a federation the constitution protects the lower tier, so the centre cannot cancel the bargain by a simple vote.

Nigeria answers that test as a federation. A written constitution divides power into exclusive functions for the federal tier, concurrent functions for federal and state tiers, and residual functions for the states. Federal law prevails where the two conflict on concurrent matters, but that supremacy does not erase the state sphere. Neither tier can abolish the other.

Centralised administration can mislead observers. Nigeria has a single national police, a Federation Account that channels oil revenue, federal roads and a presidency that dominates national attention. Those features pull power toward Abuja, yet they do not make the structure unitary. A federal constitution can still share revenue, staff offices and publicity unevenly; only the abolition test decides the form.

Confederation fails that same test from the opposite side. Its units keep sovereignty, decide by agreement and retain a right of withdrawal, so the centre cannot command them within their own states. A federal centre may be strong, but it governs units that the constitution guarantees. A confederal centre is weak before units it cannot overrule.
bullets: Ask who can abolish whom; tiers alone do not prove federalism.
Nigeria divides power into exclusive, concurrent and residual lists.
A single police and a central revenue account do not erase the bargain.
Confederal units keep sovereignty and a right of withdrawal.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why federations centralise and confederations stall
paragraphs: Federations rarely stay neatly divided. Railways, currency, defence, inter-state security and national markets create pressure for common rules, while minorities inside each state demand federal protection from the state majority. New functions therefore drift upward, especially when the centre controls the tax base that pays for them. Centralisation is less a betrayal than an outcome of money and mobility.

Nigeria shows that mechanism clearly. Oil revenue gathered in the Federation Account, a federal police and the military era’s habit of governing by decree all strengthened federal institutions at the expense of state autonomy. A strong centre can arbitrate between states, fund national infrastructure and protect rights from a hostile state government, but each intervention also teaches state actors to look to Abuja rather than to their own legislatures.

Confederations face the mirror problem. A centre that cannot tax, conscript or compel must ask sovereign members to agree, and unanimity gives each member a veto. Defence plans wait, trade rules fragment and one holdout can block the rest. The Articles of Confederation era in America illustrated the stall, which is why it was replaced by a constitution that created a centre able to act.

The comparison explains why the labels survive. Federalism must manage a permanent tension between autonomy and coordination, while confederalism must survive chronic weakness in urgent matters. A JAMB question that mentions a veto and a right of withdrawal is pointing to the confederal weakness; one that mentions a written division and a supreme court is pointing to the federal bargain.
bullets: Money, markets and security push federations toward the centre.
Nigeria’s Federation Account and single police pull power upward.
Confederal unanimity grants each member a veto.
Veto plus withdrawal signals confederal weakness; amendment plus review signals federalism.

content.heading: Go deeper: Quasi-federal Nigeria and the traps in between
paragraphs: Nigeria is often called quasi-federal because practice leans toward the centre while the text remains federal. State creation, revenue control and the legacy of military decrees gave the federal government tools that a classic federation distributes more evenly. Practice can look unitary even when the constitution still guarantees state powers.

Edge cases blur the textbook from the other side. A unitary state with elected regional councils and real budgets may behave like a federation while remaining unitary in law. A federation whose states depend on federal transfers may keep residual powers on paper while lacking money to use them. Apply the legal test before the impression.

Structure also sits beside form and system. Form asks who holds the top office, a president in a republic or a monarch in a monarchy. System asks how the executive meets the legislature, as in presidential or parliamentary arrangements. Structure asks how the centre shares power with units. Nigeria thus combines a federal structure, a republican form and a presidential system.

Decentralisation and devolution need the same care. Delegating administration that the centre can recall is decentralisation within a unitary frame. Transferring authority the centre cannot abolish is federal devolution. If the centre appoints governors or dissolves assemblies, the structure is not federal, however many tiers it contains.
bullets: Nigeria’s centre is strong, but its states remain protected.
Elected local bodies do not by themselves make a state federal.
Form, system and structure ask different questions.
Recallable delegation is decentralisation; protected power is federal devolution.

lessons.title: Nigerian Federalism: Dividing Power
lessons.objective: Explain the rationale for Nigerian federalism, the tiers and legislative lists, state creation, and the problems and corrective measures.

content.heading: Federalism in one sentence
paragraphs: Nigerian federalism divides power between a federal government and state governments, each protected by the constitution within its own sphere.

content.heading: Why Nigeria is a federation
paragraphs: A state wants to set its own school curriculum while the federal government runs defence and the currency. Both can act, because the constitution gives each level its own powers and neither can abolish the other. That is federalism.

K. C. Wheare defined the federal principle as a division of powers between a general government and regional governments, each coordinate and independent within its sphere. Nigeria adopted it in 1954 because the country was large and divided into peoples who feared domination by one another.
The constitution divides power by lists. The exclusive list belongs to the federal government alone: defence, currency and foreign affairs.
The concurrent list is shared: education and health. The residual list is left to the states. Where federal and state laws conflict on a concurrent matter, the federal law prevails.
bullets: Exclusive: federal only. Concurrent: shared. Residual: states.
Federal law prevails on a concurrent matter.
Courts arbitrate disputes between the levels.
content.takeaway: Federalism was a bargain among Nigeria's regions, not a gift from the centre.

check.question: Subjects on which both the federal and state governments may legislate are listed in the ______.
check.why: The concurrent list is shared; the exclusive list is federal only and the residual list is left to the states.

content.heading: From three regions to thirty-six states
paragraphs: At independence Nigeria had three regions; the Mid-West was added in 1963. Soldiers and later civilians kept breaking the regions into smaller states, because groups inside them demanded their own government.

Gowon created twelve states in 1967, Murtala Mohammed nineteen in 1976, Babangida twenty-one in 1987 and thirty in 1991, and Abacha thirty-six in 1996. The 1996 batch was Bayelsa, Ebonyi, Ekiti, Gombe, Nasarawa and Zamfara.

Below the states sits local government, the third tier, with 774 councils. The 1976 reforms gave councils a guaranteed share of the Federation Account, which made them depend on the centre rather than on local rates.
bullets: 1996: Bayelsa, Ebonyi, Ekiti, Gombe, Nasarawa, Zamfara.
Local government is the third tier, with 774 councils.
content.takeaway: State creation has been the main answer to demands for local autonomy.

check.question: Which of the following states were created in 1996?
check.why: Gombe and Ekiti were created in 1996; Osun and Akwa Ibom came in 1991, and Adamawa and Kogi in 1991.

visual.caption: State creation moved from 12 states in 1967 to 36 in 1996, mostly under military governments.

content.heading: The problems federalism creates
paragraphs: A census result is disputed, a state demands more oil revenue, and two states quarrel over a boundary. These are the recurring problems of Nigerian federalism: population counts, revenue allocation, boundaries and ethnic competition for power.

The constitution answers some of them. The Federal Character Principle requires appointments to reflect Nigeria's diversity; the Revenue Mobilisation Allocation and Fiscal Commission recommends how the Federation Account is shared; and derivation gives oil-producing states a share of the mineral revenue taken from their area.

The solutions are imperfect. Federal character can reward indigenes over competence, derivation leaves non-oil states poor, and revenue sharing keeps states dependent on the centre. That dependence is why Nigeria is often called a federation with strong centralising tendencies.
bullets: Problems: census, revenue, boundaries, ethnic competition.
Federal Character Principle: diversity in appointments.
RMAFC and derivation: how the Federation Account is shared.
content.takeaway: Nigeria's federal problem is less the division of power than the division of money.

check.question: Nigeria's federalism is often measured against the classical federal principle associated with ______.
check.why: Wheare's definition of coordinate governments, each independent in its sphere, is the standard test used in Nigerian textbooks.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Do not confuse the lists: exclusive is federal only, concurrent is shared, residual is states. On a concurrent matter the federal law prevails only to the extent of the inconsistency.

content.problem: The federal government sets a national minimum standard for secondary schools and a state passes a lower standard. Which law prevails, and what may the state still do?

steps.reason: Education is on the concurrent legislative list, so both levels may legislate.
steps.predictPrompt: What happens when they conflict?

steps.reason: On a concurrent matter the federal law prevails to the extent of the inconsistency.
steps.predictPrompt: What exactly does the question want you to write down first?

steps.reason: Federal supremacy applies only where the laws are inconsistent.
steps.result: The state may add stricter rules that do not contradict the federal standard.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.question: Nigeria has 36 states and 774 councils, yet it is called a federation with a strong centre. Give two features that make it federal and two that pull power to the centre.
hints: Federal features: a written constitution, coordinate levels, a supreme court, state legislatures.
Centralising features: oil revenue and the Federation Account, federal roads and police, military-era decrees.
Pair each feature with its effect on state autonomy.

content.heading: Go deeper: How the legislative lists decide who may act
paragraphs: Suppose a State House of Assembly passes a law on what the constitution reserves for the federal government alone, for example policing or currency. That law fails before its content is tested, because the state has no power at all in the exclusive field. The lists therefore decide who may act before they decide whose law is better.

The shared or concurrent field works differently. Both the National Assembly and a State House of Assembly may legislate, so the question moves from who may act to what happens when they disagree. The constitution answers that question with a narrow rule: federal law prevails only to the extent of the inconsistency.

Inconsistency does not mean duplication. A federal minimum standard for a concurrent subject does not forbid a state from adding stricter rules that do not contradict it, nor from operating above the federal floor. Duplication is allowed; contradiction triggers supremacy.

The mechanism depends on courts to define the boundary. A state that believes a federal law covers the field too broadly can test it in court, while the federal government can challenge a state law that invades an exclusive field. The Supreme Court, sitting as Nigeria's final arbiter, must decide whether a genuine inconsistency exists or whether federal power is simply being used to occupy the whole field.
bullets: Exclusive field: only federal power exists; a state law there is void.
Concurrent field: both may legislate; federal supremacy applies only where rules conflict.
Residual field: the states retain power unless the constitution removes it.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why state creation returned in 1967, 1976, 1987, 1991 and 1996
paragraphs: The three-region structure at independence concentrated power in large, rival regions. A group that lost every election inside its region had no smaller government to look to, so its leaders demanded a separate state inside the region. State creation was therefore presented as a remedy for domination.

Each military regime used the same instrument for its own reasons. Gowon created twelve states in 1967 to break the Eastern Region's power and to secure loyalty. Later regimes created states to reward supporters, to defuse a crisis, or to show responsiveness without opening the whole federation to renegotiation.

The 1999 Constitution as amended made new-state creation harder than a decree. A request must pass through the affected communities, a referendum, and approval by the state assemblies, the National Assembly and the President before it takes effect. That procedure expresses a post-military bargain: the centre can no longer draw new boundaries by announcement alone.

More states did not guarantee more autonomy. Each new state required a governor, a house of assembly, senior officials and a share of the Federation Account, while depending on federal transfers for survival. State creation eased demands for recognition but multiplied the institutions that must be funded from the same pool.
bullets: State creation began as a remedy for regional domination.
Military regimes used new states to secure loyalty and defuse crises.
The 1999 Constitution requires local consent and legislative approval for a new state.

content.heading: Go deeper: Money, population and the politics of sharing
paragraphs: Nigeria collects most of its revenue at the centre, especially from oil, and shares it through the Federation Account. States and local councils therefore depend on a monthly allocation decided largely in Abuja. The Revenue Mobilisation Allocation and Fiscal Commission recommends the formula, but dependence shapes every argument about it.

Derivation gives oil-producing states a share of mineral revenue taken from their area. That rule recognises that the states bear the environmental and social costs of production, but it also creates a sharp divide between producing and non-producing states. Non-oil states argue that derivation rewards accident of geology rather than need.

Population is the other input to the formula, which is why census exercises are disputed. A state that reports a larger population expects a larger share of allocations and more seats. Disputes over counting are therefore disputes over money and representation, not only over headcounts.

The Federal Character Principle tries to spread federal appointments across states and zones, but it can reward indigeneship over qualification and can exclude citizens who live and work outside their state of origin. The tension between fair sharing and merit remains the recurring cost of the federal bargain.
bullets: Oil revenue is collected centrally and shared through the Federation Account.
Derivation rewards production; population drives other shares and seats.
Federal Character spreads appointments but can weaken merit and resident rights.

lessons.title: Systems of Government: Presidential, Parliamentary and Monarchical
lessons.objective: Distinguish presidential, parliamentary and monarchical systems, and separate systems from structures of government.

content.heading: System in one sentence
paragraphs: A system of government describes how the executive and legislature relate, not who holds the title of ruler.

content.heading: A president elected on a separate ballot
paragraphs: A president is elected separately from the assembly, appoints ministers who need not sit in it, and serves a fixed four-year term. When the assembly rejects his budget, neither side falls; they negotiate or wait for the next election.

This is the presidential system: the executive and legislature are separately elected, the president is both head of state and head of government, and ministers answer to him rather than to parliament. Nigeria and the United States work this way.

Its merits are stability, clear accountability and strong checks between the arms. Its demerits are gridlock when the president and the majority differ, the risk of a personality cult, and the cost of separate elections.
bullets: Executive elected separately from the legislature.
President is head of state and head of government.
Fixed term; removal only by impeachment.
content.takeaway: A presidential executive stands or falls on its own election.

check.question: A system in which the president is both head of state and head of government is ______.
check.why: In a presidential system one elected president carries both titles; a parliamentary system separates the two roles.

content.heading: A prime minister who must keep the House
paragraphs: A prime minister sits in parliament, builds a cabinet from MPs, and resigns when the House defeats the budget or passes a vote of no confidence. The head of state, a monarch or ceremonial president, stays out of the fight.

This is the parliamentary system: the executive is drawn from and answerable to the legislature, ministers are usually MPs, and the government survives only while it holds the confidence of the majority. Britain and India work this way.

Its merits are unity between executive and legislature, fast legislation and flexible removal of a failing government. Its demerits are instability when coalitions break, a weak separation of powers, and executive dominance of the chamber.
bullets: Executive drawn from the legislature.
Survives only while it holds the majority's confidence.
A vote of no confidence can bring it down.
content.takeaway: A parliamentary executive holds office at the pleasure of the legislature.

check.question: In a parliamentary system, the executive is ______.
options: drawn from and answerable to the legislature
check.why: The prime minister and cabinet come from the legislature and fall if they lose its confidence.

content.heading: A king who rules, a king who reigns
paragraphs: A king rules by decree in one state; in another, the king opens parliament but does not choose the government. The first is an absolute monarchy, the second a constitutional monarchy.

In a constitutional monarchy the monarch is head of state while a prime minister drawn from parliament governs; the monarch reigns but does not rule. In an absolute monarchy the monarch is both head of state and government, and little limits him.

Systems are not structures. Unitary, federal and confederal describe how power is shared between centre and regions: a confederal union keeps the centre weak, so political stability is usually low. Nigeria is a federal republic with a presidential system.
bullets: Absolute monarchy: the monarch rules; constitutional: the monarch reigns.
Presidential and parliamentary describe the executive.
Unitary, federal and confederal describe the centre-region structure.
content.takeaway: Systems describe the executive; structures describe the centre-region split.

check.question: A major feature of a confederal state is that ______.
options: there is supremacy of the constitution
citizens owe allegiance to the centre
check.why: A confederation keeps the centre weak and the units sovereign, which makes stability hard to hold.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Form = who rules; system = how the executive and legislature relate; structure = how centre and regions share power. A country can be a constitutional monarchy and a parliamentary democracy at once.

content.problem: Classify each case: (a) Nigeria, where the president is elected separately from the National Assembly; (b) the United Kingdom, where the prime minister leads the majority party in Parliament under a monarch; (c) a league of states whose centre cannot tax or command them.

steps.reason: A separately elected president who is head of state and government is presidential.
steps.predictPrompt: Where does the executive sit in the United Kingdom?

steps.reason: A prime minister drawn from Parliament, under a ceremonial monarch, is a parliamentary system and a constitutional monarchy.
steps.predictPrompt: Which part of the question does this step answer?

steps.reason: A centre that cannot tax or command its units is confederal, a structure rather than a system.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test this answer before writing it down?

content.question: Nigeria's president is both head of state and government, and the National Assembly is separately elected. Name the system and one check the legislature has on the executive.
hints: Separate election of the executive and legislature is the presidential marker.
The Senate confirms ministers, and the National Assembly can override a veto.
A strong answer names the system and a specific check, not just 'checks and balances'.

content.heading: Go deeper: Gridlock and instability — the two opposite risks
paragraphs: A presidential system separates the election of the executive from the election of the legislature. When the president and the assembly majority belong to different parties, neither can remove the other at will. The result is not collapse but negotiation, delay and public blame that continues until the next election.

That friction is the price of stability. The president holds a fixed term, ministers remain in office through a budget dispute, and a government cannot fall mid-term merely because a coalition breaks. Critics call the delay gridlock, but supporters call it the protection that prevents a temporary majority from sweeping away a government.

A parliamentary system reverses the risk. The executive sits inside the legislature, so when a coalition breaks or a no-confidence vote succeeds, the government falls at once. Legislation moves quickly when the cabinet holds the majority, but a small swing in seats can produce repeated elections or a caretaker government.

Exam questions test the direction of the risk. A defeated chief executive who remains in office until the next election signals a presidential system; a prime minister who must resign after losing the confidence of the house signals a parliamentary system. The sequence that follows a defeat, not the title of the leader, reveals the system.
bullets: Presidential risk: gridlock because neither side can remove the other.
Parliamentary risk: instability when the majority withdraws confidence.
Fixed term signals presidential stability; confidence signals parliamentary survival.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why Nigeria left the parliamentary road in 1979
paragraphs: Nigeria's First Republic operated a parliamentary arrangement in which governments depended on regional coalitions in the federal legislature. When a regional party could block the centre or sponsor defection, the federal cabinet faced the same instability that the presidential system is meant to avoid.

The Constitution-making process that produced the 1979 text treated that experience as a lesson. By electing a president directly for a fixed term, the founders sought a single national leader who would not require a parliamentary majority to survive, and who would stand as a symbol of unity above regional competition.

The change was institutional, not only personal. A directly elected president replaced the ceremonial head of state, ministers ceased to need seats in the National Assembly, and the Senate was given a separate role in confirming appointments. The structure was designed to make a government formed after the election capable of completing its programme.

The choice also created new risks. A president who wins the national election still needs the National Assembly to pass laws and vote funds. When that assembly is hostile, the president can veto but cannot legislate. The founders accepted that friction as a safer defect than the constant removal of governments that the earlier arrangement produced.
bullets: First Republic parliaments depended on fragile regional coalitions.
A directly elected fixed-term president promised national stability.
The new risk is gridlock with a hostile National Assembly.

content.heading: Go deeper: When titles mislead — republics, monarchies and juntas
paragraphs: The word president can describe three different arrangements. In a presidential republic the president governs. In a parliamentary republic the president is ceremonial and a prime minister governs from the assembly. In a military junta an officer may title himself president while ruling by decree without any separate election.

The same warning applies to the word king. A monarch who chooses the government and issues decrees on his own stands at the head of an absolute monarchy. A monarch who opens parliament and appoints the leader of the majority party as prime minister reigns in a constitutional monarchy and belongs to a parliamentary system.

Nigeria illustrates why the title alone is insufficient. The country is a republic because its head of state is elected, not hereditary, and it is presidential because the president is separately elected and governs. During military rule Nigeria remained a republic in name but was not operating a presidential system.

For the examination, always separate three questions: who is the head of state, who is the head of government, and how does each acquire and keep office. A hereditary head of state combined with a parliamentary head of government is a constitutional monarchy; an elected head who governs is a presidential republic, whatever the army calls itself.
bullets: The title president does not decide the system.
A hereditary head with an elected prime minister is a constitutional monarchy.
Nigeria is a republic and presidential because its elected president governs.

lessons.title: The Civil Service and Public Service
lessons.objective: Explain the civil service, its control and problems, and distinguish it from the wider public service.

content.heading: Civil service in one sentence
paragraphs: The civil service is the permanent staff of ministries; the public service is wider and includes corporations and councils.

content.heading: The ministry that outlasts the minister
paragraphs: A new minister arrives with a reform plan and finds the same files, the same procedures and the same officials who served the last government. That continuity is the civil service.

The civil service is the permanent administrative arm of government, organised into ministries and departments and headed by a permanent secretary. Its defining features are permanence (officials stay when governments change), political neutrality (they serve whichever party wins), anonymity (ministers take public credit and blame), merit (recruitment by qualification) and hierarchy (orders pass down a chain).

Its functions are to advise ministers on policy, implement decisions, keep records, prepare budgets and estimates, and provide continuity between governments. It also supplies the information on which parliament and the public judge policy.
bullets: Permanence: officials stay when governments change.
Neutrality: they serve whichever party is in power.
Anonymity and merit: ministers answer publicly; recruitment is by qualification.
content.takeaway: The civil service is the part of government that does not change at an election.

check.question: The civil service is described as permanent because ______.
options: its officials keep their posts when governments change
its officials can never be dismissed
it is established directly by the constitution
it is funded from the Consolidated Revenue Fund
check.why: Permanence means continuity across governments, not life tenure: officials can still be dismissed for misconduct.

content.heading: Two heads at the top of a ministry
paragraphs: A minister announces a new policy; the permanent secretary turns it into instructions, staffing and a budget. One is the political head, the other the administrative head, and a question that asks for the administrative head wants the permanent secretary.

Control over the service is layered. Internally, hierarchy and written rules check each officer. Externally, the minister and cabinet direct policy, the legislature votes funds and questions spending, the courts review illegal acts, and the Auditor-General audits accounts.
The Civil Service Commission handles appointment, promotion and discipline, while the Public Complaints Commission investigates maladministration.

The service is also expected to be impartial: it may explain the costs of a party's promise, but it may not campaign for that party. When it is politicised, appointments reward loyalty, advice is shaped to please the minister, and the service loses public trust.
bullets: Minister: political head. Permanent secretary: administrative head.
Civil Service Commission: appointment, promotion and discipline.
Auditor-General: accounts. Public Complaints Commission: maladministration.
content.takeaway: Political direction stops where administration begins.

check.question: The administrative head of a ministry is the ______.
check.why: The minister is the political head; the permanent secretary runs the ministry's administration and advises on policy.

content.heading: The civil service is not the whole public service
paragraphs: A ministry, a state water corporation and a local council all pay staff from public funds, but only the ministry's staff are civil servants. The public service is the wider category.

The public service includes the civil service, employees of public corporations and parastatals, local government staff and other public bodies. A public corporation is created by statute as a separate legal person with its own board, accounts and powers, which lets it deliver water, power or transport more flexibly. Its staff are public servants but not civil servants.

The service's problems are red tape, corruption, poor pay, overstaffing, weak record-keeping and political interference. Reform usually targets pay, training, digital records and audit rather than abolition, because a modern state cannot run without a career administration.
bullets: Public service = civil service + corporations + councils.
Public corporation: separate legal person with its own board and accounts.
Problems: red tape, corruption, poor pay, political interference.
content.takeaway: Every civil servant is a public servant, but not every public servant is a civil servant.

check.question: A public corporation differs from a government ministry because it ______.
options: is a separate legal person with its own board and accounts
check.why: A corporation is created by statute with its own legal personality, board and accounts; a ministry is a department of the government itself.

visual.caption: Political direction travels down the administrative line, and reports travel back up.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: A public corporation is not a ministry, and its staff are not civil servants. The Civil Service Commission appoints, promotes and disciplines civil servants; it does not appoint a corporation's board.

content.problem: Classify each worker: (a) an administrative officer in a federal ministry; (b) an accountant in a state water corporation; (c) a revenue officer employed by a local government council.

steps.reason: Staff of a ministry are the core civil service.
steps.predictPrompt: Is the corporation's accountant a civil servant?

steps.reason: A public corporation is a separate legal person, so its staff are public servants but not civil servants.
steps.result: (b) Public servant, not a civil servant.
steps.predictPrompt: What could go wrong at this step, and how do you prevent it?

steps.reason: Local government staff belong to the public service, not the civil service.
steps.result: (c) Public servant, not a civil servant.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.question: Why does democracy need a politically neutral civil service, and what happens when it is not neutral?
hints: Governments change, but administration must continue without disruption.
A partisan service rewards loyalty over competence and politicises advice.
A strong answer links neutrality to continuity, impartial advice and public trust.

content.heading: Go deeper: How anonymity and neutrality make advice possible
paragraphs: A minister must defend a decision in public, answer questions in the legislature and face criticism at election time. The officials who advised that minister remain anonymous. That division allows a minister to say that the government decided, while the officer who drafted the options does not become a public antagonist of the government.

Neutrality makes the division workable across elections. A permanent secretary who has served one party must serve its successor with equal diligence, even when the new minister reverses the earlier policy. The officer's loyalty is to the office and to lawful instruction, not to a party programme.

The limit of obedience is legality. An official may explain the cost of a policy, warn that it is unworkable, and record that warning, but may not refuse a lawful decision the minister insists upon. What the official must refuse is an unlawful instruction, such as spending without appropriation or falsifying a record.

When neutrality collapses, advice changes its character. Appointments begin to reward loyalty, files are shaped to please the minister, and criticism is treated as sabotage. The public then loses the reliable information on which it judges policy, and the minister loses a check that might have prevented a costly mistake.
bullets: Anonymity lets ministers answer publicly while advice stays private.
Neutrality requires equal service to successive governments.
Lawful instruction must be obeyed; unlawful instruction must be refused.

content.heading: Go deeper: Who controls the controller — audits, commissions and courts
paragraphs: Control begins inside the ministry. A permanent secretary allocates work among directors, directors supervise units, and written rules govern recruitment, promotion and discipline. Hierarchy catches error early because each officer reviews the work of the officer below before it reaches the minister.

External control follows a different path. The National Assembly votes funds through appropriation, questions ministers on spending, and can investigate through committees. A ministry that spends beyond its vote or for a forbidden purpose faces queries, surcharges and political sanction.

After spending, the Auditor-General audits the accounts and reports on whether public money was properly applied. The Civil Service Commission and the various service commissions handle appointments, promotions and discipline, while the Public Complaints Commission investigates maladministration that citizens bring to its notice.

Courts provide the final check. An officer who is dismissed without a hearing, or who is ordered to perform an unlawful act, can seek redress in court, and a court can quash an unlawful decision or compel performance of a duty. No single controller is supreme; each watches a different transaction.
bullets: Internal hierarchy reviews work before it reaches the minister.
The National Assembly controls funds before and after spending.
The Auditor-General audits; commissions discipline; courts review illegality.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why public corporations blur the civil service boundary
paragraphs: A ministry is a department of government with no legal existence apart from the government itself. A public corporation is created by statute as a separate legal person with its own board, accounts and powers. That personality lets it own property, contract in its own name and continue when ministers change.

The device suits services that need operational flexibility. A water, power or transport corporation can set charges, hire specialist staff and manage projects at commercial pace without passing every decision through a ministry hierarchy. Its staff assist public purposes but are appointed under the corporation's own scheme, not through the Civil Service Commission.

The National Assembly may create, merge or abolish a corporation, and may require reports from its board. The relevant minister sets broad policy and approves budgets, while the board manages day-to-day operations. That split between policy control and operational management is the corporation's defining bargain.

The boundary remains a trap in examinations. A worker in a corporation and a worker in a ministry both receive public funds, but only the ministry officer is a civil servant. A local government council and a parastatal also sit outside the core civil service, even though their workers are public servants.
bullets: A corporation is a separate legal person created by statute.
Its board manages operations while the minister sets policy.
Corporation staff are public servants, not civil servants.

lessons.title: Principles of Democratic Government: Limiting Power
lessons.objective: Explain the rule of law, separation of powers and checks and balances, and the accountability conventions that keep government within limits.

content.heading: Principles in one sentence
paragraphs: Democratic government rests on principles that stop power from becoming arbitrary: the rule of law, separation of powers and accountability.

content.heading: No punishment without a law
paragraphs: A governor orders a critic detained without charge. A court frees the critic and orders the governor to pay costs, because no one may be punished except for a breach of the law proved in court. That is the rule of law.

A. V. Dicey gave it three limbs: no punishment without a breach of law proved in court; equality before the law, with no exemption for officials; and rights that arise from court decisions, not a document alone. The rule applies wherever law is supreme, not only in Western democracies.

Its remedies are writs. Habeas corpus orders a jailer to produce a detained person; mandamus compels a public authority to perform its duty; certiorari quashes an unlawful decision; prohibition stops a tribunal exceeding jurisdiction.
The right to seek redress is the right to approach a court for a remedy.
bullets: No punishment without a breach of law.
Officials answer in the same courts as citizens.
Writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari, prohibition.
content.takeaway: The rule of law means the same law binds the governor and the governed.

check.question: An order compelling a lower court or public authority to perform its public duty is called ______.
check.why: Mandamus commands performance of a public duty; habeas corpus challenges detention and certiorari quashes a decision.

content.heading: Three arms, each watching the others
paragraphs: The legislature makes law, the executive implements it and the judiciary interprets it. When one arm also does another's job, liberty is at risk; Montesquieu argued that separating them prevents tyranny.

Separation of powers is not isolation. Each arm checks the others: the president vetoes a bill and the assembly can override; the Senate confirms ministers and judges; the assembly can impeach the president; the courts can void a law or an executive act as unconstitutional.

The doctrine is never pure. Delegated legislation lets the executive make rules, and courts make law through precedent. What matters is that no single arm can both make, execute and judge the same decision.
bullets: Legislature makes, executive implements, judiciary interprets.
Checks: veto, override, confirmation, impeachment, judicial review.
No arm should make, execute and judge at once.
content.takeaway: Separation divides the work; checks and balances stop any arm from dominating.

check.question: Which power lets a court cancel a law that conflicts with the constitution?
check.why: Judicial review tests a law against the constitution; the veto belongs to the executive and impeachment to the legislature.

content.heading: Who answers when policy fails?
paragraphs: A minister approves a contract that wastes public money. Individually, he must explain and may resign; collectively, the cabinet shares responsibility for the government's policy and falls together if it loses the assembly's confidence.

Individual responsibility makes each minister answerable for his own department. Collective responsibility makes the cabinet present a united front and keep cabinet disputes private. Both depend on a legislature that can question and remove.

Constitutionalism is the wider principle: government must act within legal limits, not merely win elections. Representative government adds that the people govern through elected agents, while centralisation and decentralisation decide how much power those agents keep at the centre.
bullets: Individual: a minister answers for his department.
Collective: the cabinet stands or falls together.
Constitutionalism: power is exercised within legal limits.
content.takeaway: Accountability names who must answer, and constitutionalism sets the limit.

check.question: The convention that ministers must publicly support cabinet decisions is called ______.
check.why: Collective responsibility requires a united cabinet in public; individual responsibility concerns each minister's own department.

visual.caption: The two conventions answer different questions: who is personally at fault, and whether the government still stands.

rows.left: Free to criticise from outside cabinet

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: The rule of law is not a Western-only idea: it operates wherever law is supreme. Separation of powers is not isolation; the arms share functions and check one another.

content.problem: Name the principle at work: (a) a court orders a jailer to bring a detained suspect before it; (b) the Senate refuses to confirm a ministerial nominee; (c) a minister resigns after his department misspends funds.

steps.reason: An order to produce a detained person is habeas corpus, a rule-of-law remedy.
steps.predictPrompt: Which principle covers the Senate's refusal?

steps.reason: The Senate checking a presidential appointment is a check and balance.
steps.predictPrompt: What does the question tell you to find first?

steps.reason: A minister answering for his own department is individual responsibility.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.question: Nigeria's president vetoes a bill, the National Assembly overrides the veto, and the Supreme Court later voids part of the Act. Which principles are at work, and why is no arm acting alone?
hints: The veto and override are checks and balances.
Judicial review tests the Act against the constitution.
The answer should show each arm limiting another, not one arm dominating.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why each writ does a different job
paragraphs: Habeas corpus answers the question of detention. A jailer, a police officer or any person who holds another must produce that person before the court and show lawful authority for the detention. If no lawful authority is shown, the court orders release. The writ therefore protects personal liberty directly.

Mandamus answers a duty that has not been performed. When a public authority refuses to carry out a duty the law imposes upon it, the court can compel performance. The writ is used against inaction, not against detention or against a mistaken decision already taken.

Certiorari answers a decision that has been wrongly taken. The court quashes the decision of an inferior court, tribunal or other authority that acted without jurisdiction or in breach of law. The distinction matters in examinations: mandamus compels an omitted act, certiorari cancels an unlawful act.

Prohibition prevents a tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction before it completes the excess. It is used to stop proceedings that a tribunal has no power to hear, while certiorari is used after the tribunal has acted. In Nigeria the High Courts and appellate courts employ these remedies to keep inferior authorities within their legal bounds.
bullets: Habeas corpus challenges detention; mandamus compels a duty.
Certiorari cancels a wrong decision; prohibition stops excess jurisdiction.
Each writ matches a different failure: detention, inaction, error, excess.

content.heading: Go deeper: Judicial review and the authority to strike down a law
paragraphs: A court exercising judicial review does not act as a legislature.
